Last week’s presence-versus-background comparison was a used-versus-available design without the vocabulary. Today it gets the vocabulary, a sampling theory for availability, and a hierarchy of scales.
The continuity is exact: an RSF fitted to use-versus-available points is the same mathematical object as a presence-background SDM. What changes is that we now have TRAJECTORIES, so availability can be defined locally and dynamically.
Everything is implemented from scratch, which is unusual for this course but right for this chapter — these estimators are all short, and all routinely treated as black boxes.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Habitat
Species-specific — a collection of environmental features and resources necessary for the occupancy of an organism.
Organism-independent — a set of environmental features representing a vegetation type, plant community, or cover type.

Hall et al. (1997) argued only the first is correct. Debate continues (Lele et al. 2013).



Close to the niche concept.

The second usage is everywhere — “wetland habitat,” “old-growth habitat” — and under Hall et al.’s definition it’s a category error, because habitat is defined relative to a species.
My advice is to be explicit about which you mean.
NICHE is a property of the species, HABITAT under definition 1 is a property of a place relative to a species. That’s the distinction we flagged before.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Habitat vs resource

Resource is a feature of the environment required for growth or reproduction. May or may not be consumed.


Resources include habitat, food, and mate.
Habitat typically excludes mate, and may or may not include food, e.g., prey are often not considered habitat for predators.


Resource is the more general term: So “resource selection” is broader than “habitat selection,” and the terms are not interchangeable even though the literature treats them as such.
The predator/prey point is a nice edge case worth a moment: is a deer habitat for a mountain lion? Under a strict reading, no — it’s a resource. Practice varies.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Selection vs preference

Habitat: A species-specific concept representing the collection of physical and biological resources that allow a species to survive and reproduce.

usually misused to refer to landcover maps.



Habitat Selection: A behavioral process of choosing resources.


Habitat Preference: Innate preference for resources in the absence of constraints (e.g., competitors, predators).


“Habitat” is a highly misused term. Many ecologists point to a landcover map and call evergreen forest “habitat.” But habitat is species-specific; a forest is habitat for a woodpecker but a barrier for a grassland bird.
Habitat selection is a behavioral choice, and the The distinction that does the most work: SELECTION is what you can estimate from observational data. PREFERENCE requires equal availability, which essentially means an experiment.
So almost every paper that reports “preference” from telemetry data is reporting selection. The words are not synonyms.
AVAILABILITY is the hard one and it’s where most of the methodological argument in this chapter lives. Note the definition includes ACCESSIBILITY — something 100 km away is not available in a day, which is the whole motivation for step selection.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity overview
Goal: use one fox and two landscapes to separate quantities that are often treated as synonyms: availability, use, probability of selection, the resource selection function (RSF), and the odds ratio.
By the end, students should be able to:

Compute \(f^A(x)\), \(f^U(x)\), \(s(x)\), and \(w(x)\) from counts
Explain why the use distribution can change when selection does not


This activity reworks the fox-and-egg example from Lele et al. (2013). The paper uses one fox in one landscape. Here the fox’s behaviour stays fixed and only the landscape changes. That one manipulation exposes the paper’s central distinction: the use distribution depends on both selection and availability, while the probability of selection depends only on the resource type.
Treat this as formative assessment. The arithmetic is simple on purpose. What you’re checking is whether students can say which quantities should change between landscapes and which should not.
Suggested warm-up before revealing anything: “If the fox’s behaviour doesn’t change, which numbers do you expect to be identical in both landscapes?” Write the predictions on the board and return to them in the debrief.

This table has the same structure as Lele et al.’s Table 1, so students can map it directly onto the paper. Each row gives three counts for one egg colour: how many eggs the fox encountered, how many it ate, and how many it left. The total rows give N (all eggs encountered) and n (all eggs eaten).

Three assumptions make the arithmetic clean. They are the same three that Lele et al. list for RSF methods: (a) Availability is correctly specified. Here we know every egg the fox encountered. Real studies rarely know (a), and (b) and (c) are behavioural claims that may not hold. The extension returns to (b).
Point out the “Left uneaten” column now. It becomes the answer to Q3, because telemetry data never contain it.

section: How to calculate per color quantities?
text:
How to calculate per color quantities?
Do Steps 1–4 for each colour in each landscape. The worked example uses the blue eggs in Lele et al.’s fox example: 851 encountered and 709 eaten, out of 1313 encountered and 863 eaten in total.










Step
Quantity
Formula
In words
Worked example




1
Available distribution
\(f^A(x) = a(x)/N\)
This colour encountered ÷ all eggs encountered
\(851/1313 = 0.6481\)


2
Use distribution
\(f^U(x) = u(x)/n\)
This colour eaten ÷ all eggs eaten
\(709/863 = 0.8215\)


3
Probability of selection
\(s(x) = u(x)/a(x)\)
This colour eaten ÷ this colour encountered
\(709/851 = 0.8331\)


4
Selection ratio (an RSF)
\(w(x) = f^U(x)/f^A(x)\)
Step 2 ÷ Step 1
\(0.8215/0.6481 = 1.268\)



Steps 2 and 3 have the same numerator but different denominators: all eggs eaten versus this colour encountered.

Walk through the worked example once, pointing to where each number comes from in Lele et al.’s Table 1. Then let pairs apply the same steps to the new data.
STEP 1, f^A(x) = a(x) / N. a(x) is the number of eggs of colour x the fox encountered, and N is all eggs encountered. It answers: if I pick an encountered egg at random, what is the chance it is this colour? In the paper, 851 of 1313 eggs are blue, giving 0.6481. Lele et al. write this as a limit as N grows, because real studies only estimate it. Like them, we treat the observed proportions as true values.
STEP 2, f^U(x) = u(x) / n. u(x) is the number of eggs of colour x eaten, and n is all eggs eaten. It answers: if I pick an egg from the fox’s stomach at random, what is the chance it is this colour? 709 of 863 eaten eggs are blue, giving 0.8215.
STEP 3, s(x) = u(x) / a(x). This is the probability of selection: of the eggs of this colour the fox found, what fraction did it eat? 709 of 851, giving 0.8331. It is the quantity the RSPF models, and it depends only on colour. We can compute it this way only because we know how many encountered eggs of each colour were left uneaten, which is the point of Q3.
The most common mistake is mixing up Steps 2 and 3. Both put “eggs of this colour eaten” on top. Step 2 divides by all eggs eaten, so it gives a share of the diet. Step 3 divides by eggs of this colour encountered, so it gives a rate of acceptance.
STEP 4, w(x) = f^U(x) / f^A(x). This is the selection ratio, also called Manly’s forage ratio. It asks whether this colour is over- or under-represented in the diet relative to its availability; above 1 means eaten more than its share. 0.8215 / 0.6481 = 1.268, the value Lele et al. report. They show the selection ratio is an RSF, meaning it is proportional to s(x). Q2 finds the constant.

How to compare?

Step

\(N/n\)
All eggs encountered ÷ all eggs eaten
\(1313/863 = 1.521\)


6
Relative selection
\(RS = s(\text{blue})/s(\text{brown})\)
Step 3 blue ÷ Step 3 brown
\(0.8331/0.3333 = 2.50\)


7
Odds of selection
\(s(x)/[1 - s(x)]\)
Chance eaten ÷ chance left; do both colours
Blue: \(0.8331/0.1669 = 4.9916\); brown: \(0.3333/0.6667 = 0.4999\)


8
Odds ratio
\(OR = \text{odds(blue)}/\text{odds(brown)}\)
Step 7 blue ÷ Step 7 brown
\(4.9916/0.4999 = 9.99\)




STEP 5, N / n. All eggs encountered divided by all eggs eaten, which is the reciprocal of the overall fraction of eggs the fox ate. In the paper’s example, 1313 / 863 = 1.521. It looks like bookkeeping here, but in Q2 students show it is the constant linking w(x) to s(x). Quick check: 0.8331 × 1.521 = 1.268, the selection ratio from Step 4.
STEP 6, RS = s(blue) / s(brown). Relative selection: how many times more likely a found blue egg is to be eaten than a found brown egg. 0.8331 / 0.3333 = 2.50. Because it is a ratio of selection probabilities, any constant that multiplies both cancels, so w(blue) / w(brown) gives the same answer.
STEP 7, odds = s(x) / [1 − s(x)]. Here 1 − s(x) is the chance that a found egg of that colour is left. The odds compare eaten with left. - Blue in the paper: 0.8331 / 0.1669 = 4.99, about five eaten for every one left. - Brown: 0.3333 / 0.6667 = 0.50, about one eaten for every two left.
STEP 8, OR = odds(blue) / odds(brown). 4.9916 / 0.4999 = 9.99, matching the paper’s 9.9852. Stress that the OR (about 10) and RS (2.5) describe the same fox but are different quantities. The two are close only when both selection probabilities are small. Q4 builds on this.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Question
A colleague notes that blue eggs made up 86% of the fox’s diet in Landscape A but only 53% in Landscape B. She concludes that the fox’s preference for blue eggs weakened. Is she right? Which quantity changed, which did not, and why?

Q1 and Q2 target use versus selection and the arbitrary constant in an RSF. Q3 and Q4 connect the toy example to real study designs: what information you need to estimate absolute selection, and how the design, not the software, determines what a coefficient means.
Push faster pairs to the extension, which introduces choice probability. It pairs well with Q1 because the answer matches a number students already computed.

text:
Use changed; selection did not

Selection vs use for blue eggs



Landscape A
Landscape B




\(s(\text{blue})\)
0.80
0.80


\(f^U(\text{blue})\)
0.862
0.533




The use distribution is selection weighted by availability:
\[f^U(x) = \frac{s(x)\,f^A(x)}{\sum_{x'} s(x')\,f^A(x')}\]

A: \(\dfrac{0.80 \times 0.70}{0.80 \times 0.70 + 0.30 \times 0.30} = \dfrac{0.56}{0.65} = 0.862\)
B: \(\dfrac{0.80 \times 0.30}{0.80 \times 0.30 + 0.30 \times 0.70} = \dfrac{0.24}{0.45} = 0.533\)

The diet shifted because brown eggs became common, not because the fox changed.

This equation is the weighted-distribution relationship Lele et al. call the key relationship. It is Bayes’ theorem. Read f^U(x) as P(type x | used). Bayes says:
P(type x | used) = P(used | type x) × P(type x) / P(used)

P(used | type x) is s(x).
P(type x) among available eggs is f^A(x).
P(used) is the overall probability that a randomly chosen available egg gets eaten. That is the sum of s × f^A over all types, which is the denominator.

The x’ in the denominator is a counter that runs over every type (blue and brown), so the denominator is the same number whatever x you’re computing. Lele et al. write it as an integral because covariates can be continuous. With two categories, the integral becomes a two-term sum.
The numbers: - A: numerator for blue = 0.80 × 0.70 = 0.56. Denominator = 0.56 + 0.30 × 0.30 = 0.65. Note that 0.65 = 650/1000 = n/N, the overall fraction of eggs eaten. - B: numerator = 0.80 × 0.30 = 0.24. Denominator = 0.24 + 0.21 = 0.45 = 450/1000.
Answer to the colleague: no. Selection is unchanged. Availability changed, and the use distribution followed. This is the error Lele et al. highlight in their Discussion: using the use distribution to judge the value of a resource type ignores what was available.
Point out the mirror image in B: brown eggs are 47% of the diet even though s(brown) = 0.30. They are heavily used but weakly selected.
Terminology note: in Johnson’s (1980) sense, preference is selection measured under equal availability. The colleague is using “preference” loosely to mean selection.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Key remarks

Use = selection × availability, renormalized. Diet composition alone cannot reveal selection.
An RSF is \(s(x)\) times a landscape-specific constant (\(N/n\) here). Compare ratios, not raw values, across landscapes.
Relative selection and odds ratios are different quantities. The study design, not the software, sets the meaning of \(\exp(\beta)\).
Absolute \(s(x)\) requires the fate of encountered units, or strong assumptions about functional form.


Model answer for the exit ticket: brown eggs were 70% of what the fox encountered in B, so even eating only 30% of them yields 210 brown eggs against 240 blue, which is 47% of the diet. High use can come from high availability rather than strong selection.
If you ran the candy activity earlier in the course, connect message 1 to the Round 2 data, where the most-used candy was not the most-selected one.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Ideal Free Distribution

At equilibrium, individuals distribute themselves across patches such that all individuals have equal fitness, leading to density-dependent habitat use.










Ideal Free Distribution explains how density-dependent competition forces animals to distribute themselves across suitable habitat patches.
Fretwell & Lucas (1970). Two assumptions: individuals are EQUAL COMPETITORS, and fitness DECLINES WITH DENSITY.
Read panel (a) as a mechanism. Everyone piles into the better habitat H1 until its fitness has dropped to match H2. Only then does anyone use H2. That threshold is N*.
Predictions of the IFD: at equilibrium all individuals have SIMILAR fitness, and habitat quality correlates with number of individuals. That second prediction is what makes density a usable proxy — under the IFD.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Ideal Despotic Distribution

Fitness differs among individuals at equilibrium. Density in poor versus rich habitat depends on competition intensity.










Ideal Despotic Distribution: an ecological model where dominant animals claim the best territories and force weaker rivals into poorer habitats
Panel (b): drop the equal-competitors assumption. Dominants depress the fitness-density curve for everyone else, so N* falls and fitness DIFFERS among individuals at equilibrium. Density in poor versus rich habitat now depends on competition intensity.
And notice: under the despotic case, density no longer cleanly indicates quality. That’s the theoretical route to Van Horne’s warning.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Extensions
Relaxing IFD’s assumptions:
- non-ideal behaviour (Shochat et al. 2005)
- despotic and preemptive settlement (Pulliam 1988; Rodenhouse et al. 1997)
- Allee effects
- species interactions and predation risk (Rosenzweig 1981)
- perceptual constraints (Abrahams 1986)
- social behaviour
- stochasticity (Morris 2003)

Key: high-quality habitats should be preferred, used more consistently over space and time, and selected more rapidly and by dominant individuals (Robertson & Hutto 2006; McLoughlin et al. 2010).


That surviving set is the practically useful part, because it gives testable predictions that don’t require the full IFD.
“Selected more rapidly and by dominants” is the one people can actually check — if older or larger individuals occupy a habitat type first, that’s evidence about quality independent of density.
Pulliam & Danielson (1991) add an important qualification: even non-ideal individuals will meet these expectations if they can gain reliable information by sampling the environment.
Also relevant to Chapter 5: theory predicts SPATIAL AUTOCORRELATION in distribution, arising from spillover into nearby habitats (McLoughlin et al. 2010). So autocorrelated telemetry data may be signal, not just nuisance.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Habitat quality, and ecological traps
Habitat quality: the extent to which a habitat promotes positive population growth, through survival and reproduction.
Ecological trap: when poor-quality habitat is preferred over better alternatives (Schlaepfer et al. 2002), leading to an “attractive sink.”
Van Horne (1983): density or abundance can be a poor indicator of habitat quality.

Selection tells you what animals CHOOSE. Quality is about demographic consequence. They can diverge, and a trap is the case where they diverge catastrophically.
Robertson & Hutto (2006) is the framework paper for evaluating trap claims — Hutto is a UM name and the paper is a useful methodological check on a concept that got over-applied.
Balance: the book notes traps may be relatively RARE in practice (Sergio & Newton 2003; Bock & Jones 2004). The concept is important; the empirical frequency is contested.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Home range and territory

Home range is the area traversed by the individual in its normal activities of food gathering, mating, and caring for young (Burt 1943)


Territory is the area defended against conspecifics or heterospecifics (Nice 1941).


The phrase doing the work in Burt’s definition is “normal activities.” It explicitly excludes exploratory forays and dispersal, which is why outlier locations are conventionally trimmed — the 95% MCP rather than the 100%.
Home range size varies with environmental conditions (resource abundance), individual traits (age, sex), and population density. So “the home range size of species X” is not a constant.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Ranges, territories, key sites
Home ranges are typically larger than territories, need not cover the same area throughout life, and can be spatially separated, e.g., breeding vs non-breeding.









Adapted from Burt (1943). Note the structure: home ranges OVERLAP, territories generally DO NOT, and each contains a key site.
That pattern is diagnostic. If your estimated “home ranges” don’t overlap at all for a territorial species, you may have estimated territories. If they overlap completely, either the species isn’t territorial or your estimator is over-smoothing — which the MCP reliably does.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Utilization distributions

the two-dimensional relative frequency distribution of an animal’s position over a given period (Van Winkle 1975).


A probabilistic representation of use within a home range. Related to the ecological neighbourhood.
Gives a spatially explicit measure of intensity of use, which can then be linked to environmental features (Marzluff et al. 2004; Hooten et al. 2013).


The key word is INTENSITY. A home-range boundary is a yes/no statement; a UD says how much time is spent where.
That distinction matters for the estimators in Lab B. An MCP gives you a boundary and no intensity. Kernel, LoCoH and Brownian bridge all give you a UD.
Marzluff et al. (2004) is worth flagging as the bridge to resource selection: regress the UD value against environmental covariates and you have a utilization-weighted RSF.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Random walks








A step is a step length d and a turning angle θ. Correlation r among successive directions turns a simple walk into a correlated one.

Simple movement models, e.g., diffusion and random walks, cannot generate stable home ranges (Borger et al. 2008). They wander without bound.
Green is the start, red the end. As r rises the path becomes directional and superficially much more like observed animal movement (Kareiva & Shigesada 1983).
Terminology worth pinning down now, because Lab D depends on it. ABSOLUTE angle is measured relative to the x-axis. RELATIVE angle — the turning angle — is the change in direction from the previous step, so zero means “kept going straight.” adehabitat and amt both report both, in RADIANS not degrees.
The Lagrangian/Eulerian distinction: diffusion models are usually applied at the POPULATION level (Eulerian), random walks at the INDIVIDUAL level (Lagrangian). GPS telemetry pushed the field toward Lagrangian.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Drivers of movement

Internal state — physiological condition, personality
Motion capacity — the biomechanics of moving
Navigation capacity — how and at what scale information is acquired; perceptual range
External environment — land use and everything else

With feedbacks among all four (Nathan et al. 2008).

Navigation capacity is the one most relevant to today, because PERCEPTUAL RANGE determines what is available to an animal at a given moment (Zollner & Lima 1997; Fletcher et al. 2013). That is precisely the availability question in a step-selection function.
The feedbacks matter and are usually ignored: the environment shapes internal state, which shapes movement, which changes the environment experienced.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Resource selection

The disporportionate use of resources relative to their availability.

Resource selection operates as a hierarchical process(Johnson 1980):

1st Order: Selection of the physical geographical range of a species.
2nd Order: Selection of an individual’s home range/territory within the species’ range
3rd Order: Selection of habitat components (e.g., forest types) within the home range.
4th Order: Actual consumption of specific resources or food items at a feeding site.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point, step, or path









Three answers to “available compared to what?”

POINT: use locations versus points drawn from some region — the MCP, the study area. Availability is global and static.
STEP: use at time t versus alternatives reachable from t-1, given observed step lengths and turning angles. Availability is LOCAL and DYNAMIC.
PATH: the whole observed trajectory versus whole random trajectories.

Zeller et al. (2012) draws this distinction because the three capture resource selection during movement very differently — which matters enormously for Chapter 9’s resistance surfaces.
Note that (a) ignores the trajectory entirely, even when you have one. That throws away information and treats temporally autocorrelated points as independent.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Study Designs

Study Designs (Thomas and Taylor 2006):

Design I: Population-level measurements; individuals are not identified.
Design II: Use measured for individual animals, but availability measured at the population level.
Design III: Both use and availability measured separately for each tracked individual.
Design IV: Repeated, paired use and local availability measurements over time.



Speaker Notes: When studying resource selection, An animal might prefer coniferous forest when establishing its home range (2nd order selection), but within that home range, it might spend most of its time in hardwood swamps (3rd order selection). Thomas and Taylor classified study designs based on whether we track individuals (Design II & III) or pool them at the population scale (Design I).

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point Selection (RSF)

Compares used coordinates directly to random available coordinates.
Formulated using selection ratios (selectivity indices like Manly’s alpha) or standard logistic regressions: \[w(x) = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k)\]


Point selection (RSF) ignores the sequential path of movement. It simply pools points and compares them to background points.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Step Selection (SSF)

Compares used locations at time \(t\) to local available locations generated from the movement trajectory at time \(t-1\).
Uses step lengths and turning angles to sample realistic alternatives.
Analyzed using conditional logistic regression (clogit in survival) to honor the matched pairs/strata.


Step Selection Functions (SSFs) are much more realistic: they ask, “At this moment, given where the animal was 30 minutes ago, why did it choose this direction instead of the other options?”

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Path Selection (PSF)

Compares the entire observed path of an individual to randomly simulated alternate pathways (e.g., using random rotations or correlated random walks).


Path selection scales this up to compare entire trajectories.

R Package

The primary package for spatial point patterns in R is spatstat.
spatstat uses three core custom classes:

ppp: Point Pattern (coordinates + marks).
owin: Observation Window (study boundaries).
im: Pixel Image (covariates or kernel densities).



spatstat is a massive, incredibly powerful package. It separates the point locations (ppp) from the boundary window (owin) because boundary shape affects Ripley’s K calculations and requires edge corrections.


library(spatstat)

# spatstat was split into sub-packages c. 2022; the umbrella package
# loads them all. Where the pieces live:
#   ppp, owin, im, quadratcount, nndist   -> spatstat.geom
#   Kest, Lest, pcf, Gest, envelope       -> spatstat.explore
#   ppm, kppm, predict.ppm                -> spatstat.model
#   rpoispp, rThomas, rMatClust, rlabel   -> spatstat.random
packageVersion("spatstat")


Spatstat is one of the best maintained packages in ecology — Baddeley, Rubak & Turner’s book (2015) is the 1000-page reference if anyone gets serious.
Worth showing because error messages will sometimes name a sub-package rather than spatstat, and students find that confusing. - The book also used rgdal::readOGR to load a boundary shapefile. That’s retired; use sf::st_read() then as.owin(), or build the owin from coordinates as we do.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The Prickly Pear Cactus

Cactus species Opuntia humifusa mapped in a 50x50m plot in Florida.
Herbivore: Coreid bug (Chelinidea vittiger), a specialist insect herbivore.
Covariate: Continuous matrix vegetation height (mapped at 2m spacing).


We’ll use a simulated representation of the Florida cactus plot to demonstrate spatstat syntax. Notice that we define the boundary as a 50x50 owin.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Simulate patterns

# A smooth vegetation-height surface, as a spatstat pixel image
gx <- seq(0.25, 49.75, length.out = 100)
gy <- seq(0.25, 49.75, length.out = 100)

# NOTE: im() wants rows = y, columns = x. outer(gy, gx, ...) gets this right.
veg_mat <- outer(gy, gx, function(yy, xx)
  22 + 7 * sin(xx / 8.5) + 5 * cos(yy / 11) - 0.004 * (xx - 25)^2)
cov_veg <- im(veg_mat, xcol = gx, yrow = gy)
plot(cov_veg, main = "Simulated vegetation height (cm)")


outer(X, Y, FUN) builds every combination of the two input vectors and applies FUN to all of them at once, returning a matrix. The result has length(X) rows and length(Y) columns. So here you get a matrix with one row per value of gy and one column per value of gx
outer(gy, gx, f) produces rows indexed by gy, which is what im() wants. spatstat’s im() expects rows = y, columns = x.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
An inhomogeneous Thomas process

set.seed(414)
W <- owin(c(0, 50), c(0, 50))

kappa <- 0.008     # parent intensity, per m^2
mu    <- 4.6       # mean offspring per parent
sc    <- 3.7       # cluster scale, m

# parent intensity depends on vegetation height -> genuine inhomogeneity
lam_mat <- kappa * exp(0.10 * (veg_mat - mean(veg_mat)))
parents <- rpoispp(im(lam_mat, xcol = gx, yrow = gy))

# Gaussian offspring around each parent 
nk <- rpois(npoints(parents), mu)
ox <- rep(parents$x, nk) + rnorm(sum(nk), 0, sc)
oy <- rep(parents$y, nk) + rnorm(sum(nk), 0, sc)
keep <- ox >= 0 & ox <= 50 & oy >= 0 & oy <= 50

cactus <- ppp(ox[keep], oy[keep], window = W)
npoints(cactus)
plot(cactus, pch = 19, cex = 0.8, main = "Simulated cactus patches")



Thomas Process: Offspring are distributed around parents using a bivariate normal (Gaussian) distribution.

Let’s say vegetation has a positive clustering effect. We built the Thomas process rather than calling rThomas(), because: First, it makes the generative model visible: parents from a Poisson process, offspring Gaussian around them. Second, rThomas() only takes a constant parent intensity, and we want parent intensity to depend on vegetation.
So we know two true facts: clustering at scale 3.7 m, and a positive vegetation effect.
Offspring landing outside the window are dropped, which is why npoints is a bit below kappa * mu * area. Print it so students see the realized n.
cactus_ppp <- rThomas(kappa=0.015, scale=4, mu=4, win=cactus_win)
Our local 0-50 coordinates sidestep that entirely — worth mentioning as a practical tip: rescale before fitting trend models.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Visualization
First-order density can be estimated using a kernel smoother with a specified bandwidth.

summary(cactus)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 3))
plot(cactus, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, main = "point locations")
#Plot kernel density intensity (bandwidth sigma)
plot(density(cactus, sigma = 3), main = "kernel intensity, sigma = 3 m")
plot(cactus, add = TRUE, pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = "white")
par(op)


summary() gives n, the average intensity, and the window. The density plot is the first-order view — where are points dense? Bright patches suggest the homogeneity assumption is shaky, which motivates Lab D. Choice of sigma matters and is arbitrary; try 1 and 6 to see. Kernel smoothing shows us areas of high local density. However, is this density variation due to small-scale clustering (second-order) or a broad environmental gradient (first-order)? Point process models will help us disentangle this.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Quadrat counts and a chi-square test
text:
Quadrat counts and a chi-square test

Q <- quadratcount(cactus, nx = 4, ny = 4)   # 12.5 x 12.5 m quadrats

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot(cactus, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, main = "counts in 4 x 4 quadrats")
plot(Q, add = TRUE, cex = 1.2, col = "firebrick")
plot(intensity(Q, image = TRUE), main = "quadrat intensity")
par(op)

quadrat.test(cactus, nx = 4, ny = 4, method = "Chisq")


A significant result means the counts are inconsistent with a homogeneous Poisson process AT THE QUADRAT SCALE YOU CHOSE. Say that qualification out loud.
This is closer to a first-order analysis, since it’s about dispersion of points among sampling quadrats rather than inter-point distances. It tells you nothing about the scale of pattern.
Live demo if you have time: rerun with nx = 2 and nx = 8 and watch the p-value move. That’s the modifiable areal unit problem, and it’s the argument for the functional statistics coming next.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
K and L, ignoring edges

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))
plot(Kest(cactus, correction = "none"), main = "(a) K(r)", legend = FALSE)
plot(Lest(cactus, correction = "none"), main = "(b) L(r), expectation = r",
     legend = FALSE)
plot(Lest(cactus, correction = "none"), . - r ~ r,
     main = "(c) L(r) - r, expectation = 0", legend = FALSE)
par(op)


Three views of the same information. Panel (a) shows why nobody plots raw K — the expected curve is a parabola.
The dashed line is the theoretical CSR expectation; spatstat labels it “Kpois” or “Lpois”. The solid line is the estimate.
Panel (c) uses the formula interface . - r ~ r, which subtracts r from every curve to put the expectation at zero. That’s the second linearization convention from earlier, and it’s the one we use for the rest of the lab because departures are easiest to read against a flat line.
All three ignore edge effects, which we fix next.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: What goes wrong at the edge?
text:
What goes wrong at the edge?
Near the study area boundary you have no information about points outside.
So a circle of radius r centred near the edge contains fewer observed points than the truth.

Uncorrected statistics are therefore biased
biased increasingly at large r, because bigger circles overlap the boundary more.


The direction of bias is predictable and worth stating: uncorrected K and L will tend to DECLINE at large r, which can masquerade as regularity at large scales.
We’ll see exactly that artefact in Lab B when we compare corrected to uncorrected curves.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Edge corrections compared

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))
plot(Lest(cactus, correction = "none"), . - r ~ r,
     main = "no correction", legend = FALSE)
plot(Lest(cactus, correction = "isotropic"), . - r ~ r,
     main = "isotropic (Ripley weights)", legend = FALSE)
plot(Lest(cactus, correction = "translate"), . - r ~ r,
     main = "translate (toroidal)", legend = FALSE)
par(op)


Compare the three at LARGE r, where they diverge. At small r they agree, because small circles rarely touch the boundary.
The uncorrected curve should bend downward at large r. Explain why: near the edge you count fewer points than exist, so the estimate is dragged down, and the bias grows with r. That downward artefact can be misread as regularity at large scales.
Isotropic and translate should agree closely on a rectangular window. On an irregular polygon they would not, and translate is the more general choice.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Is it significant? Monte Carlo envelopes
text:
Is it significant? Monte Carlo envelopes
To test for non-randomness, we fit the L-function and compare it to Monte Carlo confidence envelopes under complete spatial randomness.

If the solid observed line climbs above the shaded gray envelope, the point pattern is statistically aggregated at those scales.


Lcsr  <- envelope(cactus, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                  correction = "translate", global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
Lglob <- envelope(cactus, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                  correction = "translate", global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Lcsr, . - r ~ r, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "L(r) - r with 99% envelopes: pointwise (grey) + global (dashed)")
lines(Lglob$r, Lglob$hi - Lglob$r, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "grey25")
lines(Lglob$r, Lglob$lo - Lglob$r, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "grey25")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


Point out how the observed solid line goes above the shaded gray envelope at distances from 2 to 12 meters. This indicates significant clustering. Ripley’s isotropic edge correction is used to weight points near the boundary.
rank = 1 means the envelope uses the min and max of the simulations. With 99 simulations that’s alpha = 0.01; with 19 it’s 0.05.
Note how much WIDER the global envelope is. That’s the multiple-testing correction: the global (simultaneous) envelope is based on the maximum deviation across all r, D = max|K(r) - Kpois(r)|, so a single excursion anywhere lets you reject.
Pointwise envelopes at a stated alpha CANNOT be used to reject the null at that alpha, because you’re testing at many distances. This is a widespread error in the published literature. Baddeley et al. (2014) and Wiegand et al. (2016) are the references; global tests are still an active area.
Report which you used. Most papers don’t.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Reading an envelope

ABOVE the band → more neighbours than the null predicts → aggregated INSIDE the band → indistinguishable from the null → no evidence against it BELOW the band → fewer neighbours than the null predicts → regular


Read the x-axis, not just the y. “Significant” is meaningless without a distance attached. The answer is always aggregated from a to b metres.
“Inside the band” is not “no pattern.” It means no pattern beyond what your null already contains.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The pair correlation function

Penv <- envelope(cactus, pcf, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                 correction = "translate", global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Penv, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "g(r), default bandwidth (stoyan = 0.15)")
abline(h = 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
plot(pcf(cactus, correction = "translate", stoyan = 0.4),
     main = "g(r), smoother (stoyan = 0.4)", legend = FALSE)
abline(h = 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


Expectation under CSR is 1, not 0 — different from L. Mark the line.
The stoyan argument sets the smoothing kernel bandwidth coefficient; default 0.15 follows Stoyan & Stoyan (1994). Raising it to 0.4 gives a less wiggly curve. That is a real analytical choice, and the wiggliness at small r in the left panel is data sparseness, not biology.
The key comparison to make out loud: g should show aggregation concentrated at SHORT distances, while L showed it extending further. The book’s numbers are L aggregated over roughly 2-13 m, g concentrated at 2-6 m. The difference is cumulation, not signal.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The G function

Genv <- envelope(cactus, Gest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                 correction = "rs", global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Genv, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "G(r): nearest-neighbour distribution")
plot(ecdf(nndist(cactus)), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     do.points = FALSE)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
       legend = "empirical ecdf of nndist()")
par(op)


Note the r axis is much SHORTER than for L or g. That’s inherent — nearest neighbour distances are by definition the shortest distances in the pattern.
correction = "rs" is the reduced-sample correction; edge handling for G works differently from K and L.
Overlaying the empirical ecdf of nndist() is a useful sanity check that spatstat is computing what you think. They should coincide.
The book’s result: nearest-neighbour distances random at very small scales (< 2 m) but closer than expected at larger scales — consistent with aggregation but with a minimum spacing, which makes biological sense for a plant with physical size.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Three functions, three answers



Function
What it said




L(r)
aggregation across a broad span of r


g(r)
aggregation concentrated at short distances


G(r)
near-random at the very smallest r, aggregated beyond




Reporting only K, or only nearest-neighbour distance, hides structure.
The G result at very small r is the interesting one: physical objects cannot overlap, so there’s an inhibition floor underneath the clustering. Two processes at two scales, and only G sees the smaller one.
Velázquez et al. (2016) audited practice and found most ecological papers use one statistic. Assign that reading with this slide in mind.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Use-availability
Chelinidea vittiger is a specialist herbivore on Opuntia. A poor disperser that shows aggregated distributions on cactus.
We want the distribution of the herbivore given the underlying distribution of cactus.
That’s a marked point pattern problem.

Here is our second player… READ THEN
Our simulation assigns the insect mark COMPLETELY AT RANDOM among cactus points, so we know the truth: no insect aggregation beyond the host plant’s.
Frame this as the availability problem. The insect can only be where cactus is. So “are insects clustered?” is nearly meaningless — of course they are, because their host is.
The right question conditions on availability. Lancaster & Downes (2004) is the methods reference for exactly this framing.
Is the insect herbivore (Chelinidea) aggregated on specific cacti, or is its distribution simply a random sample of the available cacti? - We use Random Labeling (rlabel) to test this. - Shuffles insect “presence” marks across the fixed cactus coordinates.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Build the marked pattern

set.seed(77)
# Insect assigned at random among cacti: TRUE pattern is random given cactus
occupied <- factor(sample(c("presence","absence"), 
                          npoints(cactus),
                          replace = TRUE,
                          prob = c(0.35, 0.65)))

cactus_PA <- ppp(cactus$x, cactus$y, window = W, marks = occupied)
table(marks(cactus_PA))

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.6, 0.6, 2.6, 0.6))
plot(unmark(cactus_PA[marks(cactus_PA) == "absence"]), pch = 1, cex = 0.8,
     main = "unoccupied cacti")
plot(unmark(cactus_PA[marks(cactus_PA) == "presence"]), pch = 19, cex = 0.8,
     main = "occupied cacti")
par(op)


Look at each mark level separately before any bivariate analysis. split() on a marked ppp will also give you one pattern per level, but passing plot arguments through plot.splitppp is unreliable, so the two panels are drawn directly here.
In the real data the mark came from six surveys per patch, truncated to presence/absence. The book does:
Note the information thrown away by truncating counts to binary. Worth a sentence: they had abundance and reduced it to occupancy for analytical convenience.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The naive analysis

bug <- unmark(cactus_PA[marks(cactus_PA) == "presence"])
npoints(bug)

Lbug <- envelope(bug, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                 correction = "translate", global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Lbug, . - r ~ r, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "Insect occurrence vs CSR (ignoring cactus)")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


This should show aggregation. And it’s an artefact — we assigned the mark at random, so there is no insect aggregation in the truth.
The apparent clustering is entirely inherited from the cactus pattern. The null here is CSR over the whole window, but the insect could never have been uniformly distributed over the window because its host isn’t.
Wrong null, wrong answer.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Condition on availability: random labelling

# Keep cactus locations fixed; shuffle which ones are occupied.
#
# envelope() controls the r grid itself: it computes the observed curve, reads
# r off it, then hands that same r to every simulation. So `fun` MUST accept an
# `r` argument (or `...`), or envelopeEngine() refuses to run.
Lpres <- function(X, r = NULL, ...) {
  Lest(unmark(X[marks(X) == "presence"]), r = r, correction = "translate")
}

Lmark <- envelope(cactus_PA, Lpres, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                  simulate = expression(rlabel(cactus_PA)),
                  global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Lmark, . - r ~ r, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "Insect occurrence vs random labelling of cacti")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


If we ignore the underlying cactus distribution, the insect appears clustered. But once we condition on cactus availability, we find that the insect is distributed randomly across available cacti.


Now the observed curve should sit inside the envelope: given where cactus is, the insect is randomly distributed. Which is the truth we built in.
rlabel() shuffles the marks while holding locations fixed — that is the null “insects occupy cacti at random.” rshift() is the alternative, performing a toroidal shift of one mark’s pattern while holding the other constant, which is the right null for a joint distribution question like competition between two species.
The book uses Lcross with random labelling here. Their call is envelope(ppp.PA, Lcross, nsim = 99, rank = 1, I = “presence”, …) with a CAPITAL I. Lcross takes lowercase i and j, so I lands in … and i silently defaults to the first mark level, alphabetically “absence”. The code does not analyse what the text says it analyses. Mine subsets explicitly to avoid the whole class of problem.
Worth flagging for anyone writing their own summary function: envelope() insists that fun accept an r argument or .... That is not fussiness. envelope computes the observed curve, reads the r grid off it, and passes that same grid to every simulation so the curves can be stacked. If you hardcode r inside your function instead of exposing it, envelopeEngine() stops with “‘fun’ should have an argument named ‘r’”.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Conclusion
Analyse the insect alone → aggregated
Analyse the insect conditional on cactus → random
Same data. The difference is the null model.

If you don’t control for resource availability, you’ll conclude the herbivore is highly aggregated. But the herbivore is actually just going where the cacti are. When you shuffle insect presence across the fixed cacti coordinates, the observed pattern falls inside the envelope!
Generalize it: whenever your points can only occur on a subset of the study area, CSR over the whole area is the wrong null. Nest sites can only be in trees. Camera detections can only be at camera locations. Captures can only be at traps.
That last one is directly relevant to the SCR work in this room — and it’s why SCR models condition on trap locations rather than treating detections as a free point pattern.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Continuous marks: is size clustered?

set.seed(31)
area_mark <- rlnorm(npoints(cactus), meanlog = log(0.4), sdlog = 0.7)
cactus_area <- ppp(cactus$x, cactus$y, window = W, marks = area_mark)

# Null = marks permuted across fixed locations. envelope()'s default null is
# CSR, which returns UNMARKED patterns that markcorr cannot use.
MCFenv <- envelope(cactus_area, markcorr, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                   correction = "isotropic",
                   simulate = expression(rlabel(cactus_area)),
                   global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(cactus_area, markscale = 1.6, main = "cactus patch area as a mark")
plot(MCFenv, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "mark correlation function")
abline(h = 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


Expectation is 1. Above 1 means large cacti near other large cacti; below 1 means large near small, i.e. an inhibition or size-asymmetry process.
We assigned area independently of location, so the curve should sit inside the envelope — matching the book’s finding of no strong spatial pattern in cactus size.
Worth asking what a real positive result would mean biologically: shared favourable microsite, or age structure from clonal spread. And what a negative would mean: asymmetric competition, where a big plant suppresses its neighbours.
Recall the variogram connection — swap m_i*m_j for (m_i - m_j)^2 and this becomes essentially next week’s tool.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
A GLM for points
An inhomogeneous point process model models the intensity of points:
\[\lambda(s) = \exp(\alpha + \beta x(s) + \dots)\]

If a point pattern varies across environmental gradients, we can model it like a spatial Poisson regression using the ppm function. - We model point intensity as a function of coordinates (Easting/Northing) or environmental rasters (e.g., vegetation height)
Formally very close to Poisson regression (Illian et al. 2008; Renner et al. 2015).
Uses: exploratory analysis, inference, and prediction/mapping.
The log link is what makes it Poisson-regression-like and guarantees positive intensity.
MaxEnt is equivalent to a Poisson point process model — so presence-only SDMs ARE inhomogeneous point process models, whether or not their users know it.
Flag that now; it reframes SDMs from a machine-learning trick into a statistical model with assumptions you can check.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Fit models

pp_int  <- ppm(cactus ~ 1)                      # homogeneous
pp_xy   <- ppm(cactus ~ x + y)                  # linear trend
pp_xy2  <- ppm(cactus ~ polynom(x, y, 2))       # quadratic trend
pp_veg  <- ppm(cactus ~ veg, covariates = list(veg = cov_veg))

data.frame(
  model = c("intercept", "x + y", "poly(x,y,2)", "vegetation"),
  npar  = c(length(coef(pp_int)), length(coef(pp_xy)),
            length(coef(pp_xy2)), length(coef(pp_veg))),
  AIC   = round(c(AIC(pp_int), AIC(pp_xy), AIC(pp_xy2), AIC(pp_veg)), 2)
)


The ppm function is the point pattern equivalent of a GLM. By comparing AIC, we can see if adding spatial trends or environmental covariates significantly improves our explanation of the point pattern’s first-order intensity.
We built a positive vegetation effect into the simulation, so the vegetation model should be well supported. If it isn’t, the effect size (0.10 in the simulation) is too small relative to n — worth saying out loud, because that’s a power lesson rather than a bug.
The book’s table: intercept 762.87, x+y 761.06, quadratic 753.31, vegetation 754.89. Quadratic best, vegetation close behind. With real data you can’t tell whether the quadratic is capturing vegetation indirectly or something else. With our simulation we know.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Predictions

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 3))
plot(predict(pp_xy2, type = "trend"), main = "quadratic trend surface")
plot(cactus, add = TRUE, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "white")
plot(predict(pp_veg, type = "trend"), main = "vegetation model")
plot(cactus, add = TRUE, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "white")
par(op)

round(coef(pp_veg), 4)


These are fitted INTENSITY surfaces — expected points per unit area. Compare them to the kernel density plot from Lab A: the density estimate is descriptive, these are model-based.
The vegetation coefficient should be positive, recovering the 0.10 we built in. Check the magnitude — it won’t be exactly 0.10 because our covariate enters the PARENT intensity, and the offspring process smears it.
That’s a genuinely instructive mismatch: the fitted model is not the generating model. A Poisson point process model assumes independence, and a Thomas process violates it. The point estimate can still be reasonable while the standard errors are too small.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Dispersion

trend_im <- predict(pp_xy2, type = "trend")

Linh <- envelope(cactus, Linhom, lambda = trend_im, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                 correction = "translate",
                 simulate = expression(rpoispp(trend_im)),
                 global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Linh, . - r ~ r, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "Inhomogeneous L: clustering beyond the fitted trend")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


Linhom is the inhomogeneous L, and the null now simulates from the FITTED trend rather than from CSR. So the question changes from “is this clustered?” to “is this clustered beyond what the trend explains?”
Because our truth is a Thomas process — real clustering at 3.7 m ON TOP OF the covariate trend — some aggregation should survive. The book finds its clustering “largely (but not entirely) accounted for.”
Compare directly to the CSR envelope from Lab B: the excursion should shrink but not vanish. That contrast is the payoff of the whole lab.
This is the general recipe: control for known drivers, then ask what pattern remains. It’s the point-pattern analogue of adding covariates to a regression.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Two cluster processes

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))

# (a) offspring dispersal kernels: Matern uniform vs Thomas Gaussian
dd <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = 400)
matern <- ifelse(abs(dd) <= 5, 1 / 10, 0)
thomas <- dnorm(dd, 0, 3.7)
plot(dd, thomas, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "grey20",
     xlab = "distance from parent (m)", ylab = "density",
     main = "(a) offspring kernels")
lines(dd, matern, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = c("grey20", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("Thomas (Gaussian)", "Matern (uniform)"))

# (b) a realization of each
set.seed(5)
plot(rMatClust(0.01, 5, 4.6, win = W), pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     main = "(b) Matern cluster realization")
par(op)


Both processes start the same way: parent points from a Poisson process, then offspring clustered around each parent.
They differ only in the offspring kernel. Matern scatters offspring UNIFORMLY within radius r of the parent — a hard edge. Thomas scatters them with an isotropic Gaussian — no hard edge, thinner tails.
Biological reading: Thomas looks like seed dispersal from a parent plant, which is why it fits the cactus data. Matern looks more like a process with a definite territory radius.
Panel (a) makes the distinction visible in one plot; the hard shoulder on the Matern kernel is the whole difference.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Fitting a cluster process as the null
text:
Fitting a cluster process as the null

fit_thomas <- kppm(cactus ~ 1, clusters = "Thomas")
fit_thomas


kppm fits a cluster process by minimum contrast. The printout gives the cluster parameters: kappa (parent intensity), scale (sigma), and mu (mean cluster size).
Compare those to what we simulated: kappa 0.008, scale 3.7, mu 4.6. Recovery won’t be exact — minimum contrast estimation is noisy on ~90 points, and our parent intensity was inhomogeneous while kppm assumes it’s constant.
The book’s fit on real data gave mean cluster size 4.6 points at scale 3.7 m, which is where our simulation parameters came from. So this slide closes the loop.
Note you can add covariates: kppm(cactus ~ polynom(x, y, 2), “Thomas”) fits clustering AND trend together, which is the better model for our data.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Envelopes under a cluster null

Env_thom <- envelope(fit_thomas, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                     global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

fit_mat <- kppm(cactus ~ 1, clusters = "MatClust")
Env_mat <- envelope(fit_mat, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                    global = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.6, 4.8, 3, 1))
plot(Env_thom, . - r ~ r, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "null = Thomas process")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
plot(Env_mat, . - r ~ r, shade = c("hi", "lo"), legend = FALSE,
     main = "null = Matern cluster process")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
par(op)


The observed curve should now sit inside both envelopes: the pattern is not distinguishable from either cluster process. Which is right — we generated it from a Thomas process.
Note the envelopes are much WIDER than the CSR envelope in Lab B. A cluster process null already contains clustering, so it takes much stronger evidence to reject it.
The deeper point, and it’s Wiegand et al. (2013)’s argument: our pattern is consistent with Thomas AND with Matern. Two different generative mechanisms, one pattern. Fitting a null well is not evidence that the null is the true mechanism.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Simulating point processes

set.seed(101)

# homogeneous, at the observed intensity
sim_hom <- rpoispp(intensity(cactus), win = W, nsim = 2)

# inhomogeneous, from a fitted ppm trend surface
sim_inh <- rpoispp(trend_im, nsim = 2)

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.6, 0.6, 2.6, 0.6))
plot(sim_hom[[1]], pch = 19, cex = 0.6, main = "homogeneous, sim 1")
plot(sim_hom[[2]], pch = 19, cex = 0.6, main = "homogeneous, sim 2")
plot(sim_inh[[1]], pch = 19, cex = 0.6, main = "from fitted trend, sim 1")
plot(sim_inh[[2]], pch = 19, cex = 0.6, main = "from fitted trend, sim 2")
par(op)


intensity() pulls lambda straight from the data, so the simulations match the observed density. Passing an im instead of a number gives an inhomogeneous process.
Emphasize what this is for. Every envelope in this deck was built from simulations exactly like these — that’s what the Monte Carlo machinery is doing under the hood. Making it explicit demystifies it.
Also: this is how you do a power analysis for a point pattern study. Simulate the effect you expect at the sample size you can afford, and see whether your statistic detects it. Nobody does this. Everybody should.
Kery & Royle (2016) is the reference for simulation-based model checking in ecology more broadly.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Recommendations
From the review you’re reading this week:

Use more than one second-order statistic — K, L, g, G to capture different information
Adjust for edge effects in almost all situations
Consider the potential for inhomogeneous patterns
Treat pointwise envelopes carefully; consider global envelopes
Remember CSR is a reference, not a hypothesis about biology


This is the practical checklist. If they internalize five things from this chapter, these are the five.
Point 4 is the one most often violated in print, and the easiest to fix.
Point 5 is the conceptual one. Rejecting CSR is nearly free — almost nothing in nature is CSR. The interesting work starts with a null that encodes something you actually believe.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Take home

The window is part of the data — change it and you change every statistic
K is cumulative; g localizes scale; G sees only the nearest neighbour
Edge effects bias you downward at large r, mimicking regularity
The null model carries the biology. Insects looked aggregated until we conditioned on their host plant
Presence-only data are thinned point data


Point 4 - If a student can articulate why the insect result changed, they’ve understood point pattern analysis better than most published users of it.

section: Exercise 1: Evaluate a Clustered Pattern against CSR
text:
Exercise 1: Evaluate a Clustered Pattern against CSR







Exercise 1


Generate a random Poisson process and a clustered Thomas process. Fit the G-function (nearest neighbor distance) for both and compare their curves.





library(spatstat)
set.seed(15)
win <- owin(c(0, 50), c(0, 50))

# 1. Simulate a completely random pattern (CSR)
ppp_random <- rpoispp(lambda=0.03, win=win)

# 2. Simulate a clustered pattern (Thomas Process)
ppp_cluster <- rThomas(kappa=0.01, scale=3, mu=3, win=win)

# 3. Calculate and plot the G-function for the clustered pattern
g_cluster <- Gest(ppp_cluster, correction="rs")
plot(g_cluster, main="G-Function (Nearest Neighbor) of Clustered Pattern")


The G-function rises very rapidly at small distances for clustered patterns because points are crowded close to their neighbors. Encourage students to compare this plot to the G-function of the ppp_random to see the difference.

Exercise 2: Fit and Predict an Inhomogeneous PPM







Exercise 2


Fit a spatial trend model to the simulated cactus dataset. Predict and map the estimated trend across the plot.





library(spatstat)
set.seed(42)
win <- owin(c(0, 50), c(0, 50))
ppp_data <- rThomas(kappa=0.015, scale=4, mu=4, win=win)

text:
Why use GLM?
A linear model describes the relationship between a response and explanatory variable(s), assuming:



The model makes biological sense
Independence of errors (blocking, mixed effects models later)
Homoscedasticity — equal variance of errors
Normality of errors

\[y = b_0   \times X_0 + b_1    \times X_1 + b_2    \times X_2 + \ldots\]

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
What is a GLM?
In a Gaussian linear model, the expected values are:


\[\mu = X \beta\]
and the errors follow a normal distribution:
\[y \sim    {Normal}(\mu, \sigma)\]






Note



But are the errors always normal? What if our response is a count, a proportion, or presence/absence?

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Model structure
Statistical models describe:

Systematic pattern in a random variable (response), possibly as a function of covariates
Random (unexplained) variability around the mean:

Response = systematic + random






Note



other pairs of terms: deterministic + stochastic, or mean + dispersion structure of model

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Key elements of a model


Deterministic process:


Stochastic process:




Why do we need both? Deterministic part is a mathematical model of a process while stochastic part is a statistical model of data that arise from the process.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Basic regression model
Deterministic process: What biological process underlies the pattern in my data?
Stochastic process: What probabilistic process produces the values of my data?
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \sim  {Normal}(0, \sigma^2)\]
is exactly the same as:
\[\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \qquad y_i \sim    {Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma^2)\]

What if the errors aren’t normal?

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Common error distributions







The family for the errors can be: Gaussian for normally distributed data

Other example error distributions include:



Poisson for count data
Binomial for success/failure data
Bernoulli for presence/absence

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
What is a GLM?
A GLM uses a link function \(L\) to describe the relationship between the mean response and the predictor:
\[L(E(y)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Linear regression
\[E(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... + \beta_n x_n\]


The link is called ”identity”
Produces μ on range (−∞, ∞)
Possibility to add interaction effects (e.g., \(\beta_3 x_1 x_2\)) and curvilinear effects (e.g., \(\beta_4 x_1^3\) )
When should we not use a linear model?
– Simple linear models produce continuous predictions across the range of all real numbers
– Equations must provide predictions matched to the biological quantities we wish to understand

Intercept-only model: simulate data
Let’s simulate observations as 1000 samples of body mass measurements of male peregrines.

rm(list = ls())
set.seed(1)
y1000 <- rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 600, sd = 30)
truth <- c(mean = 600, sd = 30)
hist(y1000, col = "grey",

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Intercept-only: frequentist
As we did last week, we can analyse these data using canned software. There are R packages to fit linear models using frequentist inference methods (e.g., lm() or glm() from stats package), or Bayesian inference (e.g., brms package).

lm1   <- stats::lm(y1000 ~ 1)
c(coef(lm1), sigma = sigma(lm1))
truth

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Intercept-only: Bayesian
We could also use general-purpose software to fit models. In this lesson, you will see how to fit linear models using R package ”nimble”. When we use R packages, we need to learn the syntax and provide the required input and format. First, make sure the required packages are installed and loaded into R. Second, bundle data in a list. Third, write the Nimble model in BUGS language.

library(nimble) # model fitting
library(coda)   # output processing

list_data <- list(mass = y1000, n = length(y1000))

model_1 <- nimbleCode({
  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:n) {
    mass[i] ~ dnorm(mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  }
  # Priors
  pop_mean ~ dunif(0, 5000)
  pop_sd   ~ dunif(0, 100)
})

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Intercept-only: Bayesian
We use Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations to draw samples from the posterior distribution of our parameters of interest. For this, we need additional input, including starting values for MCMC chains, parameters we want monitored, and MCMC settings.

inits  <- list(pop_mean = rnorm(1, 600), pop_sd = runif(1, 1, 30))
params <- c("pop_mean", "pop_sd")
ni <- 3000; nb <- 1000; nc <- 4; nt <- 1

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Intercept-only: Bayesian
We generated starting values and saved them in a list, saved a vector of the parameter names, and finally, determined how many MCMC chains and iterations we need, how many samples to keep, and how many samples to discard. Now, we can fit this model:

out1 <- nimbleMCMC(code      = model_1, 
                   constants = list_data,
                   inits     = inits,
                   monitors  = params,
                   nburnin   = nb,
                   niter     = ni, 
                   thin      = nt,
                   nchains   = nc,
                   summary   = TRUE,
                  samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Intercept-only: Bayesian
The model output will be a list. To show its contents we could use lapply(), as shown below. You should always inspect the model outputs.

lapply(out1, head)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
coda::traceplot(out1$samples)
out1$summary$all.chains # Posterior summaries from all 4 chains

section: Linear regression with covariate: simulate data
text:
Linear regression with covariate: simulate data
Let’s generate some data, including a response (body mass measurements of male peregrines during cold months) and a continuous covariate, e.g., temperature in Celsius.

set.seed(1)
truth <- c(a = 600, b = -0.5, mean = 0, sd = 10)
x   <- runif(1000, 1, 10)
eps <- rnorm(length(x), truth["mean"], truth["sd"])
y   <- truth["a"] + truth["b"] * x + eps
plot(y ~ x, pch = 19, col = "grey")


Note that we do not measure eps in reality; we measure x.
Visualizing the resulting data in this example is similar to visualizing the data you collected in the field (y) in addition to your explanatory variable (x).

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Linear regression with covariate: frequentist
Let’s use the same function as before to fit the regression line that describes the relationship between response and explanatory variables.

lm2   <- stats::lm(y ~ x)
summary(lm2)
plot(y ~ x, pch = 19, col = "grey")
abline(lm2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
# show the residuals
fit <- predict(lm2)
segments(x, fit, x, fit + residuals(lm2))

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Linear regression with covariate: Bayesian
As before, we need to bundle data in a list and write the nimble model in BUGS language. We generate starting values and save them in a list, save a vector of the parameter names, and finally, determine how many MCMC chains and iterations we need, how many samples to keep, and how many samples to discard.

list_data <- list(mass = y, n = length(y), temp = x)

model_2 <- nimbleCode({
  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:n) {
    # Response y distributed normally
    mass[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sd)
    # Linear predictor
    mu[i]   <- a + b * temp[i]
  }
  # Priors
  a  ~ dunif(0, 5000)
  b  ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
  sd ~ dunif(0, 100)
})

inits  <- list(a = rnorm(1), b = rnorm(1), sd = runif(1, 1, 10))
params <- c("a", "b", "sd")
ni <- 4000; nb <- 2000; nc <- 4; nt <- 1
# Model fitting
out2 <- nimbleMCMC(code      = model_2,
                   constants = list_data,
                   inits     = inits,
                   monitors  = params,
                   nburnin   = nb,
                   niter     = ni,
                   thin      = nt,
                   nchains   = nc,
                   summary   = TRUE,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE
)
out2$summary$all.chains

text:
Linear regression with covariate: frequentist
We can also use the glm() fucntion to fit the regression line.

glm2  <- stats::glm(y ~ x)         # identity link = same as lm()
summary(glm2)
c(coef(glm2), sigma = sigma(glm2))
plot(y ~ x, pch = 19, col = "grey")
abline(glm2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
fit <- predict(glm2)
segments(x, fit, x, fit + residuals(glm2))


The default is “identity” link. What if the response is not continuous?

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Exponential model
\[log(E(y)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... + \beta_n x_n\]


Models quantities that are only positive
Produces μ on range (0, ∞)
Preserves the additive simplicity of linear
“We used a log-transformed response variable”
“We used a linear model with a log link”

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Poisson GLM: simulate data
Relationships with count data as the response can be modeled using Poisson GLM. A logarithmic link is used between the expectation of the response (i.e., the mean count) and the predictor function (i.e., the combination of parameters on the right side of the regression equation). As a result, exponentiated coefficient estimates are the multiplicative effect on the count (response) of one unit increase in the predictor.

set.seed(500)
n           <- 300
habitat     <- factor(rep(c("forest", "grassland"), each = n/2))
temperature <- runif(n, -5, 25)

a <- 1; b_hab <- 1.5; b_temp <- 0.1; b_temp2 <- -0.005
truth <- c(a = a, b_hab = b_hab, b_temp = b_temp, b_temp2 = b_temp2)

lambda <- exp(a +
              b_hab  * (habitat == "grassland") +
              b_temp  * temperature +
              b_temp2 * temperature ^ 2)
set.seed(300)
count  <- rpois(n, lambda)

plot(count ~ temperature,
     col = habitat,
     pch = 19,
     cex = 0.6)
legend("topleft",
       legend = levels(habitat),
       col = 1:2, 
       pch = 19,
       bty = "n")

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Poisson GLM: frequentist
We can use glm() to fit a generalized linear model to count data by specifying the “poisson” link. Similar to a linear model, we can make predictions as below.

glm3 <- stats::glm(count ~ habitat + temperature + I(temperature^2),
                       family = "poisson")
summary(glm3)

new_data <- expand.grid(habitat = levels(habitat), temperature = -5:25)
new_data$fit <- predict(glm3, newdata = new_data, type = "response")
plot(count ~ temperature, col = habitat)
for(h in c("forest","grassland")) {
  lines(fit ~ temperature,
        new_data[new_data$habitat == h, ],
        type = "l",
        lwd = 2,
        col = habitat)
}

fit <- predict(glm3, type = "response")
segments(temperature,
         fit,
         temperature,
         fit + residuals(glm3,
                         type = "response"))

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Poisson GLM: Bayesian
We can fit the same model using nimble():

# Bundle data
list_data <- list(count   = count,
                  n       = length(count),
                  habitat = as.numeric(habitat) - 1,
                  temp    = temperature)
# Model code
model_2 <- nimbleCode( {
  # Likelihood
  for(i in 1 : n) {
    # Response y is from Poisson distribution
    count[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    # Linear predictor
    log(lambda[i]) <- a +
                      b_hab * habitat[i] +
                      b_temp * temp[i] +
                      b_temp2 * temp[i] ^ 2
  }
  # Priors
  a ~ dunif(0, 10)
  b_hab ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
  b_temp ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
  b_temp2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
} )
# Initial values
inits <- list(a = rlnorm(1),
              b_hab = rnorm(1),
              b_temp = rnorm(1),
              b_temp2 = rnorm(1))
# Parameters monitored
params <- c("a", "b_hab", "b_temp", "b_temp2")
# MCMC settings
ni <- 10000 ; nb <- 5000 ; nc <- 4 ; nt <- 1
# Model fitting
out2 <- nimbleMCMC( code      = model_2,
                    constants = list_data,
                    inits     = inits,
                    monitors  = params,
                    nburnin   = nb,
                    niter     = ni,
                    thin      = nt,
                    nchains   = nc,
                    summary   = TRUE,
                    samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

text:
Logistic regression
\[logit(E(y)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... + \beta_n x_n\]


Models quantities that are proportions
Produces μ on range (0, 1)
Preserves the additive simplicity of linear
“We used a linear model with a logit link”

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Logistic regression: simulate data
Let’s simulate a different response. When the response is a probability, a proportion, or a success/failure, we can fit logistic (or binomial) regression. Here we simulate data with a binary response (0/1) and two predictors, one continuous (age) and one categorical (sex). We then fit a logistic regression model and use it to make predictions.

set.seed(2007)
n   <- 1000
sex <- factor(sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.7)))
age <- runif(n, 0, 15)
# Specify odd-ratios
or_sex <- 0.5; or_age <- 1.3
truth  <- c(a = qlogis(0.3),
            b_sex = log(or_sex),
            b_age = log(or_age))

# True survival probability
surv_p <- plogis(qlogis(0.3) +
                 log(or_sex) * (sex == "M") +
                 log(or_age) * age)
set.seed(2009)
surv <- rbinom(n, 1, surv_p)
plot(surv ~ age,
     col = sex,
     pch = 19, 
     cex = 0.3,
     ylab = "Survived (0/1)")

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Logistic regression: frequentist
We can fit a logistic regression model using the glm() function. We need to specify the family as ”binomial”.

glm4 <- glm(surv ~ sex + age, family = "binomial")
summary(glm4)
exp(coef(glm4))   # odds ratios
#The estimated intercept (as a probability)
exp(coef(glm4)[1])/(exp(coef(glm4)[1]) + 1)

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Predictions: logistic regression
We can make predictions from this model. As before, we create a new dataframe and use the predict function.

new_data     <- expand.grid(sex = levels(sex), age = 0:15)
new_data$fit <- predict(glm4, newdata = new_data, type = "response")

plot(surv ~ age,
     col = sex,
     pch = 19, 
     cex = 0.3,
     ylab = "Pr(survival)")
for (s in c("M", "F")) {
  lines(fit ~ age,
        new_data[new_data$sex == s, ],
        lwd = 2, 
        col = ifelse(s == "M", "black", "red"))
}
legend("topright",
       legend = c("M", "F"),
       col = c("black", "red"), 
       lwd = 2, 
       bty = "n")


Note that type = “response” in predictions from Poisson and logistic regression.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Logistic regression: Bayesian
We can fit the same model using nimble().

list_data <- list(surv = surv,
                  n = length(surv),
                  sex = as.numeric(sex) - 1,
                  age = age)

model_3 <- nimbleCode( {
  # Likelihood
  for(i in 1 : n) {
    # Response y is from Binomial distribution
    surv[i] ~ dbern(p[i]) # the same as dbinom(p[i], 1)
    # Linear predictor
    logit(p[i]) <- a + b_sex * sex[i] + b_age * age[i]
  }
  # Priors
  a ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
  b_sex ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
  b_age ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
} )

# Starting values
inits <- list(a = rnorm(1),
b_sex = rnorm(1),
b_age = rnorm(1))
# Parameters monitored
params <- c("a", "b_sex", "b_age")
# MCMC settings
ni <- 10000 ; nb <- 5000 ; nc <- 4 ; nt <- 1
# Model fitting
out3 <- nimbleMCMC(code      = model_3,
                   constants = list_data,
                   inits     = inits,
                   monitors  = params,
                   nburnin   = nb,
                   niter     = ni,
                   thin      = nt,
                   nchains   = nc,
                   summary   = TRUE,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)
out2$summary$all.chains

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Predictions: logistic regression

new_data <- expand.grid(sex = levels(sex), age = 0:15)
# Compute posterior means -----
a_mean <- out3$summary$all.chains["a","Mean"]
bage_mean <- out3$summary$all.chains["b_age","Mean"]
bsex_mean <- out3$summary$all.chains["b_sex","Mean"]
new_data$binary_sex <- (as.numeric(new_data$sex) - 1)
new_data$fit <- cbind(ilogit(a_mean +
                             new_data$binary_sex * bsex_mean +
                             new_data$age * bage_mean ))
plot(surv ~ age, col = sex)
for(s in c("F","M")) {
  lines(fit ~ age,
        new_data[new_data$sex == s,],
        type = "l",
        lwd = 2,
        col = sex)
}


Can you add a legend to this plot to show what colors represent?

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Predictions: logistic regression
We can compute 95% Bayesian credible intervals around predictions.

a_lci <- out3$summary$all.chains["a","95%CI_low"]
bage_lci <- out3$summary$all.chains["b_age","95%CI_low"]
bsex_lci <- out3$summary$all.chains["b_sex","95%CI_low"]
