with simulation we can set a TRUE scale of effect and ask whether the method recovers it. That is impossible with the real data, where nobody knows the answer.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Custom functions









The core idea: terra stores a grid, its extent, its resolution, and its CRS in one object. We are keeping the grid as a plain matrix and the cell-centre coordinates as two vectors, cx and cy. That is all a raster is once you drop the CRS.
Orientation convention, stated once so nobody has to guess later. m[i, j] is row i, column j. Column j sits at x-coordinate cx[j]; row i sits at y-coordinate cy[i]. Row 1 is the south edge, not the north. terra uses the opposite convention, which is why its cells fill from the top left and ours do not.
make_grid — (seq_len(nside) - 0.5) * cell gives cell centres, not edges. For 200 m cells the first centre is at 100 m, the second at 300 m. Using edges here is the classic half-cell offset bug.
show_grid — image() wants z[i, j] to sit at (x[i], y[j]), which is the transpose of our convention, hence t(m). asp = 1 keeps cells square. The text() call needs the label order to match as.vector(m), which is column-major with the row index varying fastest — so cx is repeated with each = (slow) and cy with times = (fast). Get those two backwards and the labels transpose silently.
block_apply — the base-R equivalent of terra::aggregate. ri and ci are group labels: for nrow = 6, fact = 2 you get 1,1,2,2,3,3. The double loop then applies fun to each block. length.out handles grids that do not divide evenly, giving a smaller final block rather than an error.
modal — most common value. sort(unique(v)) then tabulate then which.max, which returns the first maximum, so ties resolve to the lowest value deterministically. This matters and comes up two slides on.
disagg_near — kronecker(m, matrix(1, f, f)) replaces each cell with an f x f block of copies. One line, and faster than any loop.
disagg_bilin — bilinear interpolation done as two passes of 1-D approx, which is what bilinear is. ti maps new cell centres into old row-index space; rule = 2 clamps at the edges instead of returning NA.
box_mean — a moving-window mean. A 2-D box filter is separable: run a 1-D filter down the columns, then across the rows, and you get the same answer for a fraction of the work. sides = 2 centres the window, which leaves NA in a border of width (w-1)/2 — the same edge overhang terra::focal produces, handled the same way.
circle — 200 points around a circle, for lines(). We no longer have terra::buffer to draw for us.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Build a toy landscape









set.seed for reproducibility. then generate a lxa landscape 36 cells drawn from a Poisson with mean 3. Poisson is used because it gives non-negative numbers, a common format for storing land-cover codes.
you could instead use rmultinom to simulate K land-cover types with specified probabilities — more realistic for categorical cover, but fiddlier.
Line by line. make_grid(6, cell = 1) gives six cell centres at 0.5, 1.5, …, 5.5 on each axis — a 6 x 6 unit landscape. matrix(rpois(36, 3), 6, 6) draws 36 counts and folds them into a 6 x 6 grid; matrix() fills down columns, on the next slide. length(toy) replaces ncell() — for a matrix the number of cells is just its length. show_grid(..., labels = TRUE) prints the value in each cell, replacing terra::text().

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Check the fill order
Matrices fill down the first column, then the next In this case row 1 is the south edge:









A tiny habit with a large payoff. Anyone who has silently transposed a raster knows why.
The general principle worth stating: when you assume something about how a data structure is organized, spend thirty seconds confirming it. Most spatial bugs are orientation bugs.
This slide differs from the book. terra fills from the top left, left to right, then down. Base R matrices fill top to bottom down the first column, then move right. Combined with our row-1-is-south convention, cell 1 lands in the bottom left and the numbers climb upward before stepping right. Point at the figure and say so — students who have used terra will expect otherwise, and the mismatch is the lesson.
Line by line. seq_along(toy) is 1:36. matrix(..., 6, 6) lays those out in fill order, so the printed labels are the fill order made visible. This is the base-R equivalent of values(toy2) <- 1:ncell(toy2).
Worth adding aloud: as.vector(m) reverses this, unrolling the matrix back into fill order. Any time you move between a grid and a vector of cell values, that is the order you are getting.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Increasing grain









Let’s aggregate and increase the grain.
fact = 2 means 2x2 blocks collapse to one cell; fact = 3 means 3x3.
Which rule to use mean/modal is not a style choice:
- continuous data (canopy cover) -> mean
- categorical data (vegetation type) -> modal
Using mean on categorical codes produces meaningless numbers — the average of “deciduous forest” (41) and “shrubland” (52) is not a land-cover type. Students do this.
Line by line. block_apply(toy, 2, mean) collapses each 2 x 2 block to its mean, turning 6 x 6 into 3 x 3. block_apply(toy, 3, modal) collapses each 3 x 3 block to its most common value, giving 2 x 2. The only thing that changes between the continuous and categorical cases is the function passed in — worth saying explicitly, because it makes the choice look like what it is: a decision about the data, not about the software.
Coarsening the grid means the cell size grows, so each aggregated grid needs its own coordinates: make_grid(3, cell = 2) for panel (b), make_grid(2, cell = 3) for panel (c). All three panels still span 0 to 6 units, which is why they can sit side by side. Forgetting to rebuild the coordinates is the most likely mistake when students adapt this.
par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) sets three panels; saving the old settings in op and restoring with par(op) afterwards keeps later slides from inheriting the layout.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Consequence of aggregation








The mean is preserved. The variance collapses.

The book reports mean 3.412 unchanged and variance falling from 2.82 to 0.86 — roughly a threefold drop from a single 2x2 aggregation.
Make them predict before revealing. Most correctly guess the mean is preserved. Almost nobody anticipates how severe the variance loss is.
Then the consequence: if your response depends on environmental variance rather than environmental mean, coarsening your grain can erase your effect entirely.
Line by line. as.vector() unrolls a matrix into its cell values in fill order — the base-R equivalent of values().
Why the mean survives and the variance does not? The mean of blockmeans equals the overall mean whenever the blocks are equal-sized, so aggregation is exactly mean-preserving here. The variance falls because averaging four draws cuts their variance by a factor of four — the within-block variation is not summarised, it is deleted.
Our numbers will not match the book’s 2.82 and 0.86 exactly. Same seed, but rpois is being called on a different grid construction, so the draws differ. The pattern — mean unchanged, variance down roughly threefold — is what to point at.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Decreasing grain









The book’s Figure 2.6. Panel (c) is the teaching moment: bilinear interpolation produces a smooth, attractive, high-resolution surface containing no information that wasn’t in panel (a).
It has manufactured plausible detail. That detail will happily enter a model and produce standard errors that look great.
Bilinear is defensible for genuinely continuous surfaces (elevation, temperature). It is indefensible for land-cover categories — interpolating between codes 41 and 52 gives you 46.5, which is nothing.
Ask: when is fabricated smoothness acceptable? Answer: when you have external reason to believe the underlying surface really is smooth.
Line by line. disagg_near uses kronecker() to replace each cell with a 2 x 2 block of identical copies — 6 x 6 becomes 12 x 12 with no new information, and panel (b) looks blocky because it is.
disagg_bilin runs approx() down the columns and then across the rows. Writing bilinear interpolation as two 1-D passes is not a shortcut; it is the definition. Worth showing on the board if you have time, because students often treat “bilinear” as a black box.
Cells are now half the original size, so make_grid(12, cell = 0.5) rebuilds the coordinates. Both new panels still span 0 to 6.
No labels on these panels — 144 numbers is unreadable. The point is the texture, not the values.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Changing extent








Growing the extent adds NA, not data.

The asymmetry is the point. Cropping discards information; extending manufactures empty space.
Increasing extent is not helpful unless you also populate the new area with data. Obvious when stated, and yet “extend then fill with zeros” is a real and damaging move — zero forest cover is a claim, not a placeholder.
Ask what the right fill is for an unsampled region. Usually NA, and then your model has to handle missingness honestly.
Line by line. Cropping is matrix subsetting. which(cx >= 2 & cx <= 4) finds the columns whose centres fall in the x-range, and the same on cy for rows; toy[ic, jc] keeps that block. drop = FALSE stops R from collapsing a single row or column to a vector — a real hazard if someone crops to a thin strip. Note that selecting by cell centre is a choice: a cell straddling the boundary is either in or out, never partial, which is the same convention terra::crop uses.
Extending is padding. Build a matrix of NA two cells larger in each direction, then write the original into the middle. The coordinate vectors need the new centres prepended and appended, hence c(-0.5, cx, 6.5).
The printed new_NA count is the argument in one number: extending added 28 cells and zero observations. Ask what would happen if you replaced NA_real_ with 0 — the grid looks complete, nothing errors, and every buffer overlapping the edge now reports less forest than it should.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
A landscape with realistic clumping









White noise smoothed twice, then thresholded. Crude but it produces the property that matters: forest is CLUMPED, so cover measured at nested radii will be correlated across scales — which is the whole difficulty of this chapter.
Pure white noise would not work. Cover in a 1 km and a 5 km buffer around the same point would be nearly uncorrelated, the scale of effect would be trivially identifiable, and the lesson would be lost.
Chapter 3 covers neutral landscape models, which do this properly.
Line by line. matrix(rnorm(nside^2), nside, nside) is 90,000 independent standard normals — pure white noise, zero spatial structure.
box_mean(r, 11) averages each cell with its 11 x 11 neighbourhood. That single operation is what creates the autocorrelation: adjacent output cells share 110 of their 121 input cells, so they cannot differ much. Running it twice roughly doubles the effective range of clumping. Change 11 to 5 or 31 and re-run to show the grain of the landscape change — it is the most instructive knob on the slide.
The ifelse(is.na(...)) line after each pass matters and is easy to miss. A centred 11-wide window cannot be computed within 5 cells of the edge, so those cells come back NA. Filling with the overall mean is crude but keeps the border usable. It must be done after each pass, not once at the end — otherwise the second pass propagates the NA border five cells further inward.
quantile(as.vector(r), 0.55) finds the value with 55% of cells below it; ifelse(r > thr, 1, 0) marks the top 45% as forest. Thresholding a smooth surface is what turns a continuous gradient into patches. Because we set the quantile directly, mean(forest) comes out at 0.45 by construction — say that out loud so nobody thinks it is a happy accident.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Place the sample sites









The margin matters: a 5 km buffer centred within 5 km of the edge would be clipped, and the cover estimate silently biased by the missing area. Real studies hit this constantly and often ignore it.
Ask what to do when real sites ARE near the edge of your map. Options: get more map, drop the sites, or correct for clipped buffer area. Quietly doing none of these is the common choice.
Line by line. extent_m is 60,000 m. runif(78, 6000, 54000) scatters sites uniformly in the interior, holding every site at least 6 km from an edge — 5 km for the largest buffer plus a kilometre of slack.
points() works directly after show_grid() because image() sets up ordinary plot coordinates in map units. This is the one real convenience of dropping terra: there is no SpatVector to construct, sites stay a plain data frame with x and y columns, and every base graphics function just works on them.
Worth connecting to the previous slide: because the landscape was built by smoothing, the edge cells were filled with the global mean and are therefore less variable than the interior. The 6 km margin keeps buffers away from that artefact too, not just off the edge of the grid.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Forest cover inside a buffer, one site
text:
Forest cover inside a buffer, one site









This is the book’s Figure 2.8 in two panels: isolate the habitat, place a buffer, count the cells, multiply by cell area.
The crop then mask idiom is worth naming explicitly. crop reduces the extent to the buffer’s bounding box — a rectangle. mask sets everything outside the actual circle to NA. Crop alone leaves you with the corners of the box, which would inflate your cover estimate.
Students forget the mask. The result looks fine and is wrong.
The idiom survives the rewrite, which is the good news. Panel (b) does crop and mask in five lines of base R and the lesson is unchanged — arguably clearer, because both steps are now visible rather than hidden inside two function calls.
Line by line. The crop is which(abs(cx - x0) <= 1000) for columns and the same on cy for rows: keep every cell centre within 1 km on each axis. That is a square, not a circle, and is exactly what terra::crop gives you.
The mask is the next three lines. dx and dy hold each selected cell’s offset from the site. The ordering is the trap: as.vector() of a matrix runs down columns with the row index varying fastest, so dy uses times = (cycles fast, once per row) and dx uses each = (repeats slowly, once per column). Reverse them and the mask silently rotates. Then in_1km[dx^2 + dy^2 > 1000^2] <- NA blanks everything outside the circle. Comparing squared distances avoids 2,601 square roots.
show_grid renders NA cells as blank, so the masked corners simply disappear — the same visual as terra.
lines(circle(...)) replaces lines(buffer(pt, width)). We are drawing the circle rather than asking a geometry library to construct it.
One genuine improvement to mention: our mask is an exact circle, tested cell by cell. terra::buffer approximates the circle with a polygon, so its cover figures are very slightly off. It does not matter here, but it is the kind of thing that matters when you need areas.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Turn that into a function









Compare to the book’s BufferCover, which had a bug: it referenced coords[i, 1] using an i from the enclosing loop rather than taking an index argument. It worked only because i happened to exist globally. This version takes x and y directly.
The book also had a copy-paste error in the loop that follows — both lines assigned to f1km, so f2km was never filled. Worth showing students as a reminder that published code carries bugs and that a for-loop with repeated lines is where they hide.
This version is simpler than either the book’s or the terra one, and worth dwelling on. The book computed cell area in hectares, buffer area in hectares, summed the forest cells, multiplied, divided, and multiplied by 100. All of that cancels. For a binary layer where 1 is forest, the mean of the cells inside the circle is the proportion of forest, so 100 * mean(...) is the whole calculation. Ask the class why before telling them — it is a good five-second question and it exposes whether they understand what the layer holds.
Two consequences worth stating. First, this only works because the layer is 0/1. If m held land-cover codes you would need mean(sub[inside] %in% c(41, 42, 43)). Second, because we take a mean rather than a sum, the result is automatically correct even when the circle is clipped by the map edge — the denominator shrinks with the numerator. The book’s version, which divides by the full analytical buffer area pi * size^2, silently under-reports for clipped buffers. That is a real improvement, not just a simplification.
Line by line. The two which() calls are the crop and reduce work enormously: for a 5 km buffer on a 200 m grid we examine roughly 51 x 51 = 2,601 cells instead of all 90,000. The dx/dy/inside lines are the mask, with the same each versus times ordering trap as the previous slide. na.rm = TRUE handles cells masked out earlier or lost to the edge.
The function takes cx and cy explicitly rather than reaching for g in the global environment. That is the discipline the book’s bug was missing.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Cover at six scales, all sites
text:
Cover at six scales, all sites









468 buffer operations (78 sites x 6 scales). With the bounding-box crop inside buffer_cover this is now fast — it was the slowest chunk in the deck under terra.
sapply over scales with mapply over sites replaces the book’s nested for-loop and sidesteps the indexing bug two slides back.
Line by line. mapply walks sites$x and sites$y in parallel, calling buffer_cover once per site; MoreArgs supplies the arguments that stay fixed across sites. sapply wraps that over the six scales and binds the results into a 78 x 6 matrix — sites down the rows, scales across the columns. dim(cover) confirms the shape, which is worth printing because everything downstream indexes it as cover[, "f2000"].
Why this is fast now: each call crops to the buffer’s bounding box before computing any distances, so a 500 m buffer touches about 36 cells rather than 90,000. Total work is roughly 700,000 distance calculations instead of 42 million.
If you switch to the real 30 m NLCD data, aggregate first — the book warns that computation time grows with buffer size, and at 30 m a 5 km buffer contains about 87,000 cells before you have done anything.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: The problem: cover is correlated across scales
text:
The problem: cover is correlated across scales

















The book’s Figure 2.9. Every pairwise scatterplot is tight and positive, and the correlation matrix confirms it — adjacent scales above 0.9, and even 500 m vs 5 km substantially correlated.
Why: a 5 km buffer CONTAINS the 1 km buffer. These are not independent measurements, they are nested ones.
This is the crux of the chapter. Everything on the next four slides is a consequence of this figure.
Line by line. Nothing changed here — cover is an ordinary numeric matrix either way, so pairs() and cor() need no adaptation. Point that out: once the raster work has produced a site-by-covariate table, you are doing plain statistics and the spatial packages are irrelevant.
labels = paste0(scales / 1000, " km") relabels the diagonal in kilometres so the panel headings read “0.5 km” rather than “f500”.
Two things to draw attention to in the correlation matrix. The values just off the diagonal are the highest, because 3 km and 4 km buffers overlap almost completely. And the whole matrix is positive — there is no scale at which cover becomes uninformative about cover at another scale, which is precisely why the next slide’s model comparison is underpowered.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Why that correlation is the whole problem
text:
Why that correlation is the whole problem
If forest cover at 1 km, 2 km, and 5 km are correlated at r > 0.9, then models using them will fit almost equally well.
“The scale of effect” is then only weakly identifiable from the data.
We can still say forest cover matters. Saying at what scale is much harder.

Make sure this lands before showing the log-likelihood profile, or students will over-read the peak.
The analogy: this is collinearity, and the usual collinearity consequences apply — coefficients are estimable but poorly separated, and model comparison between near-identical predictors is low-powered.
Tie back to Jackson & Fahrig (2015): if the data barely distinguish scales, the reported scale of effect will be driven by which scales the analyst chose to test. Their meta-analytic result is exactly what this figure predicts.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Simulate presence with a KNOWN scale of effect
text:
Simulate presence with a KNOWN scale of effect








Now we know the answer is 2 km. Can the standard method find it?

This is what simulation buys us and the real data cannot. The book fits its models and reports that 2 km is best supported, but nobody knows the skink’s true scale of response, so there’s no way to evaluate the method.
Using the book’s own estimates (-6.16, 0.0856) means our simulated dataset has a comparable prevalence and effect size, so the figures look like Fig 2.11.
Ask students to predict now: will the log-likelihood peak at exactly 2 km? Take a show of hands, then reveal.
Line by line. cover[, "f2000"] pulls the 2 km column — percent cover, on a 0 to 100 scale, which is why the coefficient 0.0856 is small. plogis() is the inverse logit, converting the linear predictor to a probability between 0 and 1. rbinom(78, size = 1, prob = p_occ) draws one Bernoulli trial per site with that site’s own probability, giving the 0/1 presence vector.
Only f2000 appears anywhere in this chunk. The other five columns exist in cover but play no causal role — that is what makes 2 km the truth rather than a label.
The added range(p_occ) line is worth printing: if the probabilities span most of 0 to 1 the design has real signal, whereas a narrow range would mean even a perfect method could not distinguish scales. Check it before drawing conclusions from the next three slides.
table(presence = pres) reports prevalence. If it comes out badly lopsided, re-seeding is legitimate — but say so out loud rather than quietly.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Logistic regression at one scale
\[\text{logit}(p_i) = \alpha + \beta \times \text{forest}_i\]









Standard logistic regression, the same model as the book’s Equation 2.1. Errors assumed binomial.
Be explicit about what this model ignores, as the book is: no detection error (MacKenzie et al. 2002), no spatial dependence (Chapters 5-6), no other covariates. It is a teaching model, not a publishable one.
The detection point is worth a minute for a wildlife audience — a naive occurrence model conflates “absent” with “present but not detected,” and the whole occupancy-modelling literature exists because of it.
Line by line. Unchanged from the book, and unaffected by dropping terra — cover is a matrix and pres a vector, so this is ordinary glm. family = binomial selects the logit link by default.
The estimate on the second row should sit near the 0.0856 we simulated from, because we are fitting at the true scale. That is the benchmark for the next two slides: everything there is a comparison against this.
logLik is the number the next slide profiles across scales. Say what it means: higher is a better fit to these data, and because all six models have the same number of parameters, comparing log-likelihoods directly is legitimate. That is why the book does not bother with AIC here.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Log-likelihood across scales









The circled point is the best-fitting scale; the dashed line is the truth.
If they coincide, say so and note it won’t always. If they don’t, that IS the lesson — with correlated predictors and 78 sites, the peak wanders. Re-render with a different seed in the presence simulation and it may move.
That instability is the honest result and worth demonstrating live if you have time: change set.seed(7) and re-run.
The book uses log-likelihood rather than AIC here, correctly noting AIC would give identical rankings because all models have the same number of parameters.
Line by line. sapply over colnames(cover) fits six separate logistic regressions, one per scale, and extracts each log-likelihood. as.numeric() strips the logLik class so the results bind into a plain vector rather than a list.
The plotting is three annotations on one line graph. abline(v = 2000) marks the truth. which.max(ll) finds the best-supported scale and points(..., pch = 1, cex = 3) rings it — an open circle rather than a colour change, so the figure survives greyscale. The text() call sits at min(ll) so the label never collides with the curve.
The printed table matters as much as the plot. Look at the spread of log-likelihood values, not just which is largest. If the six numbers fall within one or two units of each other, the data barely distinguish the scales, and the circled winner is close to arbitrary. That is the honest reading and the plot alone hides it.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
But look at the coefficients









The book’s key observation: coefficient estimates are nearly IDENTICAL across scales of 2 km and above. Only at 500 m is the relationship notably weaker.
So the practical conclusion is split: - “forest cover increases skink occurrence” -> well supported - “the scale of effect is 2 km” -> weakly supported
Those deserve different levels of confidence in a paper, and are routinely given the same.
If any CI here crosses zero, note that 78 sites is a small dataset for this question — another honest limitation.
Line by line. fit_one refits the model at one scale and returns three numbers: the slope and a Wald 95% interval, est +/- 1.96 * se. The as.numeric() calls are not cosmetic — summary()$coefficients[2, ] is a named vector, and without stripping the names, sapply would carry “Estimate” through and the explicit colnames() assignment two lines later would fight with it. This is a real bug I have hit; leave the comment in the code.
t(sapply(...)) gives one row per scale and three columns. Setting colnames explicitly rather than relying on whatever sapply inherited is the defensive move.
arrows(..., code = 3, angle = 90) draws the error bars — a two-headed arrow with flat ends is the base-R idiom for a confidence interval, since there is no errorbar() function.
The reading to insist on: the points are flat from 2 km rightward and the intervals all overlap heavily. A flat profile with overlapping intervals says the data cannot separate these scales. Contrast that with the previous slide’s single circled winner, which implies far more precision than exists.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Buffers vs kernels









The buffer is a step function: a cell 1,999 m away counts fully, a cell 2,001 m away counts not at all. Stated that way, nobody would defend it as a model of organism perception.
The kernel weights nearby cells more, decaying smoothly. Sigma controls how fast.
Note the deeper advantage on the next slide: sigma is ESTIMATED from the data rather than chosen by the analyst, which removes the a priori binning that Jackson & Fahrig identified as the dominant driver of reported scales of effect.
Line style varies as well as colour, so the figure survives greyscale printing and colour-blind viewers.
Line by line. No raster here at all — this slide is pure illustration and needed no rewriting. d is a sequence of distances from 0 to 6 km.
buf_w is the buffer’s weight function: 1 inside 2 km, 0 outside, then divided by its own sum so it integrates to 1. gauss is the same normalisation applied to a Gaussian. Dividing by the sum in both cases is what makes the three curves comparable — otherwise a wide kernel would sit lower simply because it is spread further.
ylim = c(0, max(gauss(d, 700))) scales the axis to the tallest curve, the narrow kernel. The buffer’s flat line looks low by comparison, which is honest: it spreads the same total weight over a wider area than the narrow kernel does.
Point at the discontinuity in the grey line. That vertical drop at 2,000 m is the modelling assumption nobody would defend if asked to state it plainly.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The Gaussian kernel weight
\[w(d_{ij} \mid \sigma) = \frac{\exp\left(-\dfrac{d_{ij}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}{\sum_{i \neq j}\exp\left(-\dfrac{d_{ij}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}\]

\(d_{ij}\) — distance from sample location \(i\) to cell \(j\)
\(\sigma\) — scale parameter, estimated from the data
Weights sum to 1, so the covariate is a weighted average of cover

Small \(\sigma\) → nearby cells dominate. Large \(\sigma\) → distant cells matter more.

This is the book’s Equation 2.3, following Chandler & Hepinstall-Cymerman (2016).
The normalization matters: dividing by the sum makes the weights a proper weighted average, so the covariate stays on a comparable scale regardless of sigma. Without it, sigma and beta would be hopelessly confounded.
Fitting requires writing the likelihood by hand, which is the next slide, and is genuinely good for students — most have only ever called glm().

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Fit it by hand with optim
text:
Fit it by hand with optim









Three things worth pausing on.
First, exp(par[1]) for sigma. Optimizers work on unconstrained space; sigma must be positive; exponentiating enforces that. Standard trick, worth naming.
Second, the negative log-likelihood. optim MINIMIZES, so you negate.
Third, truncation. The full site-by-cell distance matrix for the real 30 m data would be 78 x 3,215,254. Setting distances above 10 km to zero and dropping all-zero columns makes it tractable. The book uses the Matrix package for genuine sparse storage; we just subset, which is enough at this resolution.
I vectorized the weighting as a matrix product rather than the book’s apply, which makes optim roughly an order of magnitude faster.
Warn students that optim can be sensitive to starting values here — the book says so too. Ours start near the buffer estimates.
The only rewritten part is the first block, and it hides the one real trap in this whole deck. as.data.frame(x, xy = TRUE) used to hand back cell coordinates and values in matching order. We now build them by hand, so the ordering has to be right or the model fits noise.
as.vector(forest400) unrolls the matrix in fill order: down column 1, then column 2. So fx must repeat each x-coordinate once per row — each = length(cy) — while fy cycles through all y-coordinates once per column — times = length(cx). This is the same each versus times pairing as the masking slide, and getting it backwards produces a distance matrix that is wrong but not obviously wrong. If you change anything here, sanity-check with plot(fx, fy, col = fv + 1) and confirm it reproduces the landscape.
block_apply(forest, 2, modal) coarsens 200 m to 400 m, cutting the cell count from 90,000 to 22,500 and the distance matrix with it. modal not mean, because forest is categorical.
outer(sites$x, fx, "-") builds a 78 x 22,500 matrix of x-offsets in one call; the same for y; then Pythagoras, divided by 1,000 for kilometres.
Everything from nll_kernel down is unchanged from the terra version. Say that explicitly — once the data are in matrices, the statistics does not care where they came from, and that is the general lesson of this rewrite.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Kernel vs buffer — does it pay?
text:
Kernel vs buffer — does it pay?









The book’s Figures 2.11c and d. Two results:
The two covariates are almost the same thing — the book reports r = 0.97, and log-likelihoods nearly identical. All that machinery to land in the same place.
And AIC often FAVOURS the buffer, because the kernel spends an extra parameter on sigma. The book reports 68.91 kernel vs 66.74 buffer.
This is a genuinely deflationary result and the book presents it honestly rather than burying it. Worth praising out loud — it models the behaviour you want from students.
Line by line. No raster operations at all; unchanged apart from reusing p_k from the previous slide instead of recomputing unname(fit_k$par).
nll_buf refits the 2 km buffer model by hand. It would be easier to call glm(), but then the two AIC values would come from different machinery, and any discrepancy would be uninterpretable. Fitting both with optim on the same negative log-likelihood makes the comparison airtight. Say that — students should see that comparability sometimes justifies more work.
2 * fit$value + 2 * length(fit$par) is AIC from a negative log-likelihood: optim already minimised -logLik, so 2 * value is -2 logLik. The kernel has three parameters against the buffer’s two, so it pays a penalty of 2.
The W reconstruction rebuilds the fitted weight matrix at the estimated sigma and applies it to get the kernel covariate. plot(cover / 100, covw) puts both on a 0 to 1 proportion scale so the 1:1 line is meaningful; the buffer covariate is stored as a percentage, the kernel one as a proportion.
The 1:1 line, not the correlation, is the thing to point at. High correlation with points off the diagonal would mean the two covariates rank sites identically but differ in level. Points on the line mean they are the same measurement.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
So why bother with kernels?
Three reasons:

More plausible — nearby locations get more weight than distant ones, which is how organisms actually work
More objective — no a priori decision about which scales to test
Quantifies uncertainty in the scale of effect — something buffer analyses simply don’t estimate

But: \(\sigma\) can be poorly determined and sensitive to starting values. More work on estimating scales of effect is needed.

Reason 2 is the strongest, and it connects directly to Jackson & Fahrig (2015). If your reported scale of effect is largely determined by the scales you chose to test, then a method that doesn’t require choosing is a real advance regardless of what AIC says.
Reason 3 matters for anyone who wants to make a claim ABOUT the scale rather than just using a covariate. A buffer analysis gives you a winner with no confidence interval.
The closing caveat is the book’s own and worth reading aloud — this is an open methodological problem, not a solved one. Good thesis territory.
On reason 3, one concrete follow-up now that we fit by hand: fit_k carries a Hessian, so sqrt(diag(solve(fit_k$hessian)))[1] gives a standard error for log(sigma), and exponentiating the endpoints of log(sigma) +/- 1.96 se gives a confidence interval for sigma itself on the kilometre scale. That is the uncertainty the buffer analysis cannot produce, and it takes one line. Worth showing live if there is time.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Roadmap for today

Point pattern and point process
Spatial randomness
Point pattern analysis


Last week, we worked with grid cells, this week we work with point locations as data and try to model how points are distributed in space. An insect that looks strongly aggregated turns out to be randomly distributed once you condition on where its host plant is.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point data

Distinct locations in space

Point data are among the most common spatial data types in ecology:

individual trees
bird nests
habitat patches
patchy disturbances such as burrows
locations of species occurrence
origin points of an invasion


Point data refers to distinct locations in space. One of the most common data types we see in spatial ecology. What are some of your point data? Camera deployments, nest sites, capture locations, telemetry fixes — though telemetry needs care, since repeated locations of one animal are not independent points.
Note the third one: habitat PATCHES as points. A patch mosaic can be reduced to a point pattern of patch centroids

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point pattern

A set of spatial coordinates of discrete “events” or individuals observed inside a specified boundary.

Typical point pattern analysis questions:

Are the points aggregated, uniform, or random?

Does that change with scale?
What process produced it?


Emphasize that PPA differs from standard spatial modeling because the point location itself is the random event under study, rather than just the attribute value at that location. We want to know: why are the points where they are?
Question 3 is the hard one, and the honest answer is often “several processes could have.”
Emphasize that 1 and 2 are descriptive and largely solved; 3 is inferential and mostly not.
Wiegand et al. (2013) is the key citation: different point processes can produce nearly identical summary statistics, which is why they argue several statistics should always be used. That paper is the reason this chapter teaches four functions instead of one.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Three processes, one pattern
How to disentangle dispersal, habitat heterogeneity, and plant-plant interactions as causes of conspecific aggregation? (Lara-Romero et al. 2016 on canvas) 

Do you have pets? Let’s say you go home and as soon as you open the door you see a broken vase on the floor. You realize that the window is open and your cat is sitting close by licking its paw. Now, all you see is a broken vase, maybe a draft blew a curtain into it, maybe the cat knocked it over, maybe someone broke in, you don’t recall if you left the window open. The pattern is the broken vase, the process could be any of these. Remmeber we talked about plants grouptogether in clusters? Using point pattern analysis we can model the underlying processes. The alternatives are: - a homogeneous point pattern process where seess are distributed at random without env preference or autocorrelation with where the trees are - Inhomogeneous poisson process where clustering is because of soil nutrients or microhabitat conditions, entirely environmental drive - Poisson cluser process where the pattern is purely as a result of dispersal from original trees - the biological process -Finally, an inhomogeneous poisson cluster process which is a combination of both biological and env.
We’ll walk through both univariate and marked point pattern analysis. We’ll be using the spatstat, which is the most comprehensive point pattern analysis package in the R ecosystem.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Spatial dispersion

The arrangement of points in space relative to one another


Aggregated (clumped): Points cluster together
Random: Points are distributed independently.
Regular (uniform): Points are evenly spaced.


library(spatstat)   # startup banner suppressed via message: false

W1 <- owin(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
set.seed(3)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(rMatClust(25, 0.05, 4, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2, 
     main = "(a) aggregated")

plot(rpoispp(100, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2, 
     main = "(c) random")

plot(rMaternII(400, 0.045, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2,  
     main = "(b) uniform (regular)")

par(op)


the three classical dispersion types. We can visually distinguish the three main forms of spatial dispersion. Panel (b) is worth pausing on — genuinely regular patterns are rare in nature and usually indicate territoriality or competition for space. - Seabloom et al. (2002, PNAS): extinction rates under non-random habitat loss differ substantially from random-loss predictions. Since real land conversion is emphatically non-random — it follows soils, slope, and roads — the standard species-area extrapolation is systematically wrong.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Dispersion is scale dependent

library(spatstat)

W1 <- owin(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
set.seed(3)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.4, 0.5))
for (s in c(0.03, 0.08, 0.18)) {
  plot(rMatClust(12, s, 8, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2,
       main = paste("aggregated, scale =", s))
}
par(op)


Pattern without scale isn’t always informative. “Aggregated” without a scale attached is nearly uninformative.
at alrger scale, an aggregated pattern looks almost uniform.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Characteristics
All the methods here need x–y coordinates of point locations, plus:

a window: the study area boundary
optionally marks: attributes of points, categorical (e.g., used vs available, predator vs prey) or continuous (e.g., biomass, height)
optionally covariates: as a pixel image, e.g., elevation.


READ then: The used/unused framing is the one that generalizes best for wildlife work: your points are available resource units, and the mark says whether they were used. That converts a resource-selection question into a point pattern question (Lancaster & Downes 2004). - That’s exactly the cactus/insect example in Lab C Introduce spatstat’s three data types now, since they structure the whole lab: ppp (point pattern), owin (window), im (pixel image).
The window is the piece students underestimate, which is the next slide.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Sensitivity to window
Assumption: the pattern was generated by a single point process over the entire study area.
So the delineation of the study area, its size and location, affects the pattern you observe.
Windows can be rectangular or highly irregular polygons.

PPA is highly sensitive to the size and shape of the study boundary
This is the extent problem.
When is this assumption violated? All the time! The single-process assumption is strong and frequently violated. If half your plot is upland and half is wetland, that is arguably two processes, and pooling them will manufacture apparent aggregation that is really a habitat boundary.
Cropping to a homogeneous subregion is the crude fix. Inhomogeneous models are the solution.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point pattern information content

set.seed(11)
Wd <- owin(c(0, 10), c(0, 10))
Xd <- rMatClust(0.12, 1.1, 4, win = Wd)
n  <- npoints(Xd)

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.4, 0.5))

# (a) points in a window
plot(Xd, pch = 19, cex = 2, main = "(a) points + window (boundary)")

# (b) bivariate mark: used / unused
used <- factor(sample(c("used", "unused"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.35, 0.65)))
plot(ppp(Xd$x, Xd$y, window = Wd, marks = used),
     cols = c("grey60", "firebrick"), chars = c(1, 19), cex = 2,
     main = "(b) bivariate mark")

# (c) continuous mark: size
sz <- rlnorm(n, log(1), 0.5)
plot(ppp(Xd$x, Xd$y, window = Wd, marks = sz),
     markscale = 0.45, main = "(c) continuous mark")

# (d) points on an underlying gradient
gg <- seq(0.1, 9.9, length.out = 60)
grad <- im(outer(gg, gg, function(yy, xx) sin(xx / 2.6) + cos(yy / 3.1)),
           xcol = gg, yrow = gg)
plot(grad, main = "(d) points on a covariate", ribbon = FALSE)
plot(Xd, add = TRUE, pch = 3, cex = 1, col = "white")
par(op)


Your point pattern could be as simple as a boundry/window and your coordinates. The points could contian categorical information such as used/unused. Or continuous information, such as group size.
Panel (b) is the resource use/availability setup. Panel (d) is the inhomogeneous case: if the covariate drives intensity, the pattern will look clustered even with no biological aggregation at all.
Panel (d) is the trap. Environmental heterogeneity and true aggregation produce the same signature in K. Distinguishing them requires either a covariate model (Lab D) or an assumption. This is the point-pattern version of the SA-env vs SA-sp distinction from Week 1’s Figure 1.2.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Poisson point process

A point process is a random process producing realizations of point patterns across space and/or time.

The most common: the Poisson point process — points are independently distributed in space, described by their intensity λ.

First-Order Intensity λ: Describes the density of points across space.
Second-Order Relationships: Relate to the spatial interaction between points (e.g., attraction, competition).


“Independently distributed” means the presence of a point at one location tells you nothing about any other location. Almost no biological process satisfies this, which is exactly why it makes a useful null.
First order: how many points, and where is density high? Second order: given a point, what’s near it?
First-order properties represent the spatial trend (large-scale density). Second-order properties represent localized interactions (small-scale clustering or competition). Intensity λ is points per unit area — roughly density. Keep the distinction between the intensity FUNCTION lambda(x), which can vary across space, and a constant lambda.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point intensity
First-Order Intensity λ: Describes the density of points across space:

Homogeneous (= stationary) — intensity is constant across the window
Inhomogeneous (= non-stationary) — intensity varies across space

Also isotropy — the process does not change with direction.

If the density is constant across the window when Density varies across spatial or environmental gradients
When inhomogeneous, the usual objective is figuring out what explains the trend.
Stationary and homogeneous are used interchangeably here. Isotropy is the directional analogue and is almost always assumed, rarely tested.
Anisotropy is real and under-examined: patterns along a river corridor, a prevailing wind, or a contour are directional. Everything today assumes it away.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Thinned point processes

A thinned point process is one where the observed points are a sample of the underlying process.

Thinning creates inhomogeneity in the intensity function independent of the underlying process from biology (e.g., mortality) or study design.

Presence-only SDM are thinned point data (Warton & Shepherd 2010), often biased near roads, which biases model predictions (Elith et al. 2006; Phillips et al. 2009).
The logic: your MaxEnt “presence points” are a road-biased, effort-biased sample of an underlying point process. Fit a model to them and you have modelled the sampling as much as the species.
Fithian et al. (2015) is the fix — estimate the thinning process by pooling survey data with opportunistic data. Renner et al. (2015) is the general treatment.
Everything else today assumes a COMPLETE CENSUS of a region, which the cactus data is and eBird is not.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Numerical summaries

Numerical summaries are global, one number for the whole study area.

e.g., mean/variance ratio of quadrat counts, against a Poisson expectation:



Relationship
Interpretation




mean > variance
regularity


mean ≈ variance
randomness


mean < variance
aggregation



But these give no information about scale, and they are contingent on how you drew the quadrats.

The Poisson has mean equal to variance, which is why the ratio is diagnostic. Overdispersion means clustering.
“Contingent on how you drew the quadrats” is the modifiable areal unit problem again. Change the quadrat size and you change the verdict.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Functional summaries

Functional summaries are curves over distance r, which is how you get at scale.

First-order: summarize points individually, no explicit relation to other points. The intensity function λ(x).
Second-order: statistical relationships estimated from information in pairs of points. Number of points within distance r of a focal point.
Higher-order statistics exist (triplets of points) but the overwhelming majority of practice is first- and second-order.

Practical version: first order asks “where are there more points?” Second order asks “given a point here, what’s within r?” Only second-order statistics can speak to interaction, which is why they dominate.
Wiegand & Moloney (2014) cover third-order statistics for anyone curious. They exist, they’re informative, and almost nobody uses them.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Complete spatial randomness

a homogeneous Poisson process: Points occur independently with constant intensity

Two assumptions:

the number of points n in a region follows a Poisson distribution with mean λ = n/A
given n, points are an independent random sample, equally likely anywhere — uniform over the study region


Part 1 is about how many. Part 2 is about where, given how many.
“it is likely that CSR rarely occurs in nature.” It is not a biological hypothesis, it is a reference point. Rejecting CSR tells you the pattern is non-random and nothing more — it does not tell you which process produced it.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Monte Carlo envelopes
Simulate complete spatial randomness many times, at the observed n. Take the range of simulated curves as a confidence envelope (Baddeley et al. 2014).
If the observed curve falls outside, there is evidence of pattern differing from complete spatial randomness.

This is the workhorse and it is conceptually simple: build the sampling distribution of your statistic under the null by brute force.
Watch out for one thing coming in Lab B: because the envelope is computed at MANY distances r, a pointwise envelope at a stated alpha cannot be used to reject the null at that alpha. That’s a multiple-testing problem and it’s pervasive in the published literature.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Other null models

Cluster point processes — assume aggregation

Matérn Cluster: “Parent” points are random; “offspring” are distributed uniformly within a radius \(r\) around parents.
Thomas Process: Offspring are distributed around parents using a bivariate normal (Gaussian) distribution.

Inhibition processes — assume regularity

Matérn Inhibition: Points are generated but deleted if they fall within a competitive threshold distance \(r\) of another point.

Environmental gradients — use a known resource gradient as the null, then ask whether points are aggregated above and beyond it (Melles et al. 2009)


The third option is where the science is. “Are these nests clustered?” is a weak question. “Are these nests clustered beyond what the distribution of suitable substrate explains?” is a real one. inhomogeneous point process
Melles et al. (2009) did exactly this for songbird nesting — disentangling habitat drivers from social drivers of nesting pattern. Directly relevant to anyone in this room working on colonial or territorial species.
Lab D and Lab E implement both routes.

text:

set.seed(21)
px <- c(5.0, 6.9, 3.3, 7.6, 4.4, 8.4, 2.4, 6.1, 3.8, 7.1)
py <- c(5.0, 6.4, 6.8, 3.6, 3.1, 6.9, 3.9, 8.1, 2.0, 5.2)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.6, 0.6, 2.6, 0.6))

## (a) K / L : everything inside a disc of radius r

        bg = "grey92", fg = "grey40")

## (b) g : a ring at radius r, smoothed
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), asp = 1)
symbols(px[1], py[1], circles = 3.6, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE,
        bg = "grey92", fg = NA)

        bg = "white", fg = NA)
symbols(px[1], py[1], circles = 3.2, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE,
        fg = "grey35", lwd = 2)

text(px[1] + 1.7, py[1] + 0.4, "r", font = 3, cex = 2)
box(col = "grey50")

## (c) G : nearest neighbour only
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), asp = 1)
points(px, py, pch = 19, cex = 2)
points(px[1], py[1], pch = 15, cex = 2.5, col = "firebrick")
d <- sqrt((px - px[1])^2 + (py - py[1])^2); d[1] <- Inf
nnb <- which.min(d)
arrows(px[1], py[1], px[nnb], py[nnb], length = 0.12, lwd = 2.5,
       col = "firebrick")
box(col = "grey50")
title("(c) G : nearest neighbour distance", cex.main = 2)

Moving away from detecting patterns by numerical summeries, we can use functional summaries. Here are three geometries, three questions.

K uses everything inside the disc, so it is CUMULATIVE.
g uses only what’s in a thin ring at r, so it is scale-LOCAL. The grey band is the smoothing kernel bandwidth.
G uses only the single nearest neighbour, so it emphasizes the shortest distances and ignores everything else.

Ask which they’d use to detect clustering at exactly 5 m but not at 10 m. Answer is g, and the reason is the cumulative-versus-local distinction that comes up three slides on.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Ripley’s K
The degree of spatial aggregation of points within a circle of radius r, compared to complete spatial randomness:
\[K(r) = \frac{E}{\lambda}\]
where λ = n/A and E = expected number of points within r of an arbitrarily chosen point, excluding that point.

K(r) larger than expected → clustering
K(r) smaller than expected → regularity


Ripley (1976). The most-used second-order statistic in ecology by a wide margin.
“Excluding that point” matters — otherwise every point contributes itself and you’d have a constant offset.
Dividing by lambda is what makes it comparable across patterns of different density. Without that, K would just track abundance.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: K under CSR, and the r² problem
text:
K under CSR, and the r² problem
Area of a circle is πr², so under complete spatial randomness the expected count is \(E_{\text{CSR}} = \lambda \pi r^2\), giving
\[K(r)_{\text{CSR}} = \pi r^2\]
That grows quadratically, which makes plots hard to read — deviations at large r dominate visually.

This is why nobody plots raw K. The expected curve is a parabola, so eyeballing departures from it is unreliable, and the vertical scale is dominated by large r.
The fix is linearization, next slide. It’s purely cosmetic in the sense that no information changes — but it makes the plot readable, which matters.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Linearizing to L — two conventions
Expectation = r: \[\hat L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi}\] aggregation if L(r) > r; regularity if L(r) < r
Expectation = 0: \[\hat L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi} - r\] aggregation if L(r) > 0; regularity if L(r) < 0
Always check which one a figure uses.

That last line is not pedantry. Both conventions are common, both are called “L”, and reading a figure under the wrong one inverts your interpretation of where the null line sits.
spatstat’s Lest uses expectation = r. To get expectation = 0 you plot with the formula . - r ~ r, which we do throughout the lab. Point that out when it first appears.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
How K is actually computed
\[\hat K(r) = A \frac{\sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} w_{ij} \, I(d_{ij} < r)}{n^2}\]

\(d_{ij}\) — distance between points i and j
\(I(\cdot)\) — indicator, 1 if \(d_{ij} < r\), else 0
\(w_{ij}\) — weight correcting for edge effects

Ignore the weights and it simplifies to counting neighbours within r, scaled by intensity.

Strip away the notation and it’s: count all pairs closer than r, scale by density and area. That’s it.
The w term is the entire edge-correction literature compressed into one subscript, and it’s the subject of three slides from now.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The pair correlation function g
\[g(r) = \frac{dK(r)/dr}{2\pi r}\]
The slope of K at radius r, divided by the circumference at r.

g(r) = 1 → CSR
g(r) > 1 → aggregation
g(r) < 1 → regularity


Because it’s a derivative, g isolates what happens AT r rather than out to r.
In practice it’s implemented either with a ring width (delta-r) or, better, with a smoothing kernel (Penttinen et al. 1992). Bandwidth is a real choice: too narrow and data sparseness makes the curve wiggle spuriously; too wide and it approaches K.
The O-ring statistic of Wiegand & Moloney (2004) is a close relative: O(r) = lambda * g(r).

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Why g beats K for identifying scale
text:
Why g beats K for identifying scale
K is cumulative — all points closer than r are used.
So strong aggregation at 5 m makes K look aggregated at 10 m too, because r = 10 still contains everything inside 5.
g is a derivative, so it localizes.
K is simply the cumulative version of g (Baddeley 2007; Velázquez et al. 2016).

This is the most practically useful methodological point in the chapter, and it shows up in the Lab B results: L suggests aggregation from 2-13 m, while g localizes it to 2-6 m. The L signal at 8-13 m is an artefact of cumulation.
Illian et al. (2008) recommend distance-based analyses either to complement or in place of K. Velázquez et al. (2016), one of this week’s readings, found ecologists still overwhelmingly report K.
If a paper reports only K and claims a scale, be sceptical.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The G function
Cumulative distribution of nearest-neighbour distances. The “event-to-event” distribution.
\[\hat G(r) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbf{1}(d_i \leq r) \qquad
G(r)_{\text{CSR}} = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)\]

G(r) > GCSR(r) → distances shorter than expected → aggregation
G(r) < GCSR(r) → longer than expected → regularity


Intuitive: the probability of finding your nearest neighbour within distance r.
The catch: it ignores everything beyond the nearest neighbour, so it captures smaller-scale structure than K, L or g. Notice in Lab B that the r axis for G is much shorter — that’s not a plotting choice, it’s inherent.
Useful side application: G gives you a way to interpret the spatial scaling of patch isolation, connecting to nearest-neighbour distance metrics from Chapter 3.
The empty-space function F is the location-focused analogue. We skip it, as the book does.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Marks: bivariate and continuous
Bivariate (cross) K — for two categorical point types:
\[\hat K_{12}(r) = A \frac{\sum_i \sum_j I(d_{ij} < r)}{n_1 n_2}\]
computed for \(K_{12}\) and \(K_{21}\), then averaged.
Mark correlation function — for continuous marks:
\[\hat K_m(r) = \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} I_r \, m_i m_j\]
Asks whether large values tend to be near other large values.

A lovely connection the book points out: replace m_i * m_j with (m_i - m_j)^2 and the mark correlation function becomes nearly equivalent to the empirical variogram, which is Chapter 5’s central tool. Same arithmetic, different tradition.
Flag that now — it makes next week feel continuous with this week rather than a fresh start.
Interpretation for the mark correlation: above 1 means large near large, below 1 means large near small.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity overview
Format: Pairs
Materials: 2 maps, 1 distance card, ruler
Suppose you have a complete census of elk across a 2km × 2km block of the Blackfoot
Your group’s job: For each distance card, determine with numbers if elk locations on the maps are aggregated, random, or regular?

Preparation:

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 1


0 - 3 minutes. Look at Map A. In one word, please write down: Are these elk clustered, random, or regular?
2 - 4 minutes. Propose a method to prove with numbers what you committed in the previous step.



Hand out Map A and give no other instructions. Do not mention distance, scale, or nulls.
Everyone will write “clustered.” That unanimity is the setup — it means the reversal in phase 4 lands on the whole room at once rather than on one unlucky group.
Harvest proposals on the board. DO NOT EVALUATE ANY OF THEM.
This phase is supposed to be uncomfortable. Two to three minutes of genuine floundering is the goal.
EXPECT THESE PROPOSALS, and write all of them up without comment:
“Count elk in squares and see if some squares have more” -> quadrats, a real method, and the one the hook uses “Measure the distance to each elk’s nearest neighbour” -> the G function, arriving spontaneously “Compare to a map where they’re spread out evenly” -> a null model, arriving spontaneously “Calculate the average distance between all pairs”
IF NOBODY MENTIONS A COMPARISON, ask: “clustered compared to WHAT?” and let the silence do the work. That question is the whole lesson, and it is far better if the room feels the need for it before you supply an answer.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 2

Here is the measurement we will make: for a typical elk, count how many OTHER elk lie within distance r of it.
To know whether that count is a lot, you need to know what randomness would have given you.



There are 60 elk in 4 km². If those 60 elk were scattered at random across the block, how many would you expect to find inside a circle of radius r?
Work it out. You have everything you need.



DO NOT HAND THEM THE FORMULA. They will get there in about ninety seconds, and it is the last thing in this activity they can own.
The route: density = 60 / 4 = 15 elk per km². Area of a circle = pi r squared. Expected = 15 x pi r squared, with r in kilometres.
RESCUE PROMPT, if a group stalls past a minute: “if there were 15 elk per square kilometre, how many sit inside a circle of 0.28 square kilometres?” That is enough; do not finish it for them.
WATCH FOR THE UNITS TRAP. Several groups will work in metres and get an answer thousands of times too big. Let them discover it by sanity-checking against the map: a 100 m circle cannot contain 47,000 elk. Units errors caught by physical plausibility are worth more than units errors caught by you.
ONCE A GROUP HAS IT, write their formula on the board in their notation and leave it up. Phase 3 refers back to it.
STILL SAY NOTHING about scale-dependence, nulls, grain, or which map to use.
IF ASKED “which r?” -> “whichever one is on your card.” IF ASKED “which map?” -> “you decide, and be ready to justify it.”

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 3


Pick a distance (m) and follow the steps below.

Measure the scale bar on each map with your ruler. Work out how many millimetres equal one metre on each map.
Decide which map your question can be answered on. Be ready to justify it.
Pick three focal elk. For each, draw a circle of radius r and count how many other elk fall inside.
Average your three counts → observed.
Compute expected, using the formula your group just derived.
Report observed ÷ expected. That ratio is your answer.




DISTANCE CARDS: 8 m, 30 m, 100 m, 500 m — one per group.
WHAT EACH RADIUS BECOMES ON EACH MAP (for you, not for them):
       Map A        Map B
8 m 0.8 mm 8 mm 30 m 3 mm 30 mm 100 m 10 mm 100 mm 500 m 50 mm off the map
WHAT WILL HAPPEN, GROUP BY GROUP.
GROUP A (8 m) tries Map A, finds 8 m is under a millimetre, and gets stuck. LET THEM STAY STUCK FOR A FULL MINUTE before nudging: “is there another map on your desk?” That moment of being unable to ask the question is discovery 3, and it is worth the discomfort.
GROUP B (30 m) has the same experience in milder form — 3 mm is drawable but uncountable, because the herd is a smudge. They should migrate to Map B.
GROUP C (100 m) on Map B will find a 100 mm radius runs off the sheet. The elegant route is to measure the herd’s greatest dimension (60 m) and realise every 100 m circle therefore contains the entire herd, so the answer is 19 without drawing anything. If a group gets there, have them present it.
GROUP D (500 m) must use Map A, because 500 m does not exist on Map B. Their circle covers a quarter of the landscape and still contains only their own cluster.
Everyone will notice they are measuring ELK TO ELK — not to a habitat edge, not a cell size. Do not say so. Ask it in phase 6.

DISCOVERY 1. Let the room fight about it. Someone will say “clustered at some distances and not others,” and when they do, write their sentence on the board VERBATIM and put their name next to it. That sentence is the chapter.
Only AFTER they have said it do you supply the vocabulary: dispersion is not a property of a point pattern, it is a property of a point pattern AT A STATED DISTANCE — which is why K, g and G are functions of r rather than single numbers.

Fill in the “From map” column as groups report, and then ask the room why the column is not all the same. The answer is discovery 3.

Here the three herds are identical by construction, so it happens to be safe. The honest answer is that checking that assumption is exactly what a real analysis does by averaging over many focal points spread across the whole window. This is a genuinely good objection — say so.

THAT TWO-MAP WORKFLOW IS THE RIGHT ANSWER and is worth naming out loud: Group D needed Map A for what is ABSENT at 500 m and Map B for what is PRESENT at close range. No single extent could answer their question.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 5
On Map B (one herd, 20 elk in a 180 × 180 m frame), we found zero neighbours within 8 m. Ratio equals 0, fewer than random.


Have we proved that elk avoid standing close together?



A close pair: two elk standing closer together than 8 m.
Before you can call zero a finding, you have to ask: would randomness have given us zero too?


Let them argue for a minute before you touch the arithmetic.
DEFINE “PAIR” OUT LOUD, because the next slide depends on it. Pick any two elk, measure between them; if that distance is under 8 m they are a close pair. The question is how many such pairs randomness would produce.
THE LOGIC TO LAND: if randomness also produces zero, then finding zero tells you nothing about elk. You have not measured the elk — you have measured the fact that 8 m is a very small circle.
Do not run this slide together with the next one. The pause between “you might have nothing” and “watch what happens when we change the window” is what makes the reversal land.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 5
Work it out for Map B, 20 elk in a 180 × 180 m frame.
density = 20 ÷ 0.0324 km² = 617 elk per km²
expected neighbours per elk = 617 × π(0.008)² = 0.124
expected pairs = 20 × 0.124 ÷ 2 = 1.24 pairs

Why divide by two? Every pair got counted twice — elk A counts B as a neighbour, and B counts A.
Randomness on Map B predicts about 1.2 close pairs. You would see zero about 29% of the time.


THE DIVIDE-BY-TWO IS THE STEP PEOPLE SKIP. Make them say why.
“1.24 PAIRS” IS NONSENSE AS A LITERAL OBJECT, so explain it as a rate: scatter 20 elk at random in this frame, count the close pairs, write it down, and repeat a thousand times. You would average 1.24 pairs per attempt — which means zero happens about 29% of the time.
That framing is far more persuasive than “1.24 is a small number.” Say it as: a zero here is roughly a one-in-three outcome under the hypothesis Group A thinks they have rejected.
WHY MAP B AND NOT MAP A. Group A counted on Map B, so the expectation has to be computed for Map B. Mixing windows — observing on one map and expecting on another — is the exact error this phase teaches, and it is easy to commit by accident. If you had used the whole-block density of 15 per km2 here you would have got 0.09 pairs and a P(zero) of 91%: same conclusion, wrong arithmetic.
The 29% figure treats close-pair counts as Poisson. Fine at this magnitude.

text:
Activity debrief







What we found
The name for it




The verdict changes with the distance you ask about
Dispersion is scale-dependent


We were measuring elk-to-elk distances. No pixel, no quadrat, no grain
r is the scale of analysis


We couldn’t ask the 8m question on a 2km map
Extent limits detectable scales


Same r, two densities, opposite results
The null model decides the answer




ASK, DON’T TELL. For each row, ask “what did we actually find out?”, write their words, then add the term beside it. The terms stick because they are labels for something the room already owns.
ROW 2 IS THE ONE THEY WILL NOT VOLUNTEER, so prompt it: “what two things were you measuring the distance between?” Elk and elk. “So what was the grain of this analysis?” There wasn’t one. Point patterns are the only data type in this course with NO GRAIN AT ALL, because exact coordinates mean there is no aggregation unit. Students arriving from Lessons 2 and 3 have been trained to hear every distance as grain or extent, and this is where you break it.
TWO OPTIONAL FOLLOW-UPS IF TIME REMAINS.
FIRST- VERSUS SECOND-ORDER. Which of the verdicts is about the environment and which about the elk? Three clusters a kilometre apart is FIRST-ORDER — intensity varies because habitat does, and it would hold even if elk ignored each other entirely. The 8 m spacing is SECOND-ORDER — points responding to other points, and it would happen in a perfectly uniform meadow.
PROCESS VERSUS PATTERN. “Same census tomorrow at 7 a.m. — same map?” No: different coordinates, same rules. The point PROCESS is the rule elk follow; the point PATTERN is where they happened to stand on Tuesday. You only ever observe the second and you are always trying to infer the first.


Dispersion is not a property of a point pattern; it is a property of a point pattern at a stated distance. That is why K, g, and G are functions of r rather than single numbers.
PROCESS VS PATTERN. “Fly again tomorrow at 7 a.m. — same map?” No: different coordinates, same rules. The point PROCESS is the rule elk follow; the point PATTERN is where they happened to stand on Tuesday. You only ever observe the second and you are always trying to infer the first.
Closing line: “Clustered compared to what?” is not a pedantic question. It is the entire chapter.

section: What goes wrong at the boundary
text:
What goes wrong at the boundary
Near the study area boundary you have no information about points outside.
So a circle of radius r centred near the edge contains fewer observed points than the truth.
Uncorrected statistics are therefore biased — and biased increasingly at large r, because bigger circles overlap the boundary more.

The direction of bias is predictable and worth stating: uncorrected K and L will tend to DECLINE at large r, which can masquerade as regularity at large scales.
We’ll see exactly that artefact in Lab B when we compare corrected to uncorrected curves.

rect(0, 0, 10, 10, border = "grey25", lwd = 2)

# wrapped copies

     font = 2)

     adj = 0, cex = 0.95)

Isotropic (Ripley 1988): if the circle is entirely inside, w = 1. If half the circumference is outside, w = 2 for points inside. Intuitive, but works poorly for irregular complex boundaries.
Translate (toroidal): wrap the window like a torus so the pattern has no edge. Works on ALL window geometries, which is why it’s the general-purpose default and what we use in the lab.
The open circles in (a) are the points you don’t get to see. That’s the whole problem in one visual.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
When not to correct
If the boundary is a hard, true boundary for the points, correcting is wrong (Lancaster & Downes 2004).
Examples: a pond edge for aquatic larvae; an island coastline; a fenced enclosure.
The correction assumes points could exist outside. Sometimes they can’t.

Good discussion prompt: is your study plot boundary real or arbitrary? Almost always arbitrary, which is why correction is almost always right — but the exceptions matter and nobody thinks about them.
A stream reach for benthic insects, a habitat patch boundary for a specialist, a lake shore. In those cases the “missing” points genuinely do not exist and inflating your counts invents them.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
What all of this assumes

Stationarity (homogeneity) — intensity constant over space
Isotropy — no directional dependence
Complete census, not a sample

The functions can be extended to inhomogeneous processes (Lab D). Isotropy usually just gets assumed.
On sampling: randomly thinning a Poisson process leaves a Poisson process, so random samples are defensible. Biased samples are not.

That last point is subtle and worth stating carefully. Random thinning preserves Poisson-ness, so a random subsample doesn’t invalidate a CSR test. Systematic or biased thinning does.
Which brings back the presence-only problem: road-biased occurrence records are biased, not random, thinning. Everything today would be invalid on them.

Roadmap for today

Habitat analysis

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Space Use and Habitat Selection

Habitat selection theory predicts how individuals choose resources to maximize fitness:

Ideal Free Distribution: Animals distribute themselves proportionally to resource availability to maximize fitness.

Key goals:

Estimate space use and home ranges from animal tracking data.
Quantify resource selection - points vs steps.



On Tues we started to talk about habitat analysis. We covered terminology, use vs selection vs preference vs available, habitat theory, and introduced resource selection function as a heterogeneous point process. Today, we We will explore how to take raw telemetry points and map individual home ranges, estimate utilization distributions, and analyze selection functions.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Selection

The disporportionate use of resources relative to their availability.

Resource selection operates as a hierarchical process(Johnson 1980):

1st Order: Selection of the physical geographical range of a species. e.g., Where within the former range should we reintroduce this species?
2nd Order: Selection of an individual’s home range/territory within the species’ range e.g., Why did this panther put its home range here rather than 20 km east?
3rd Order: Selection of habitat components (e.g., forest types) within the home range. e.g, Within its home range, why does it rest in palmetto thickets?
4th Order: Actual consumption of specific resources or food items at a feeding site. e.g., Which individual deer does it kill?


I showed you GPS tracks of 6 Florida panther individuals.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Study Designs

Study Designs (Thomas and Taylor 2006):

Design I: Population-level measurements; individuals are not identified. i.e., Animal density along a forest-cover gradient; no marked individuals
Design II: Use measured for individual animals, but availability measured at the population level. i.e., Individual GPS fixes vs one study-area availability layer
Design III: Both use and availability measured separately for each tracked individual. i.e., Individual GPS fixes vs availability inside each animal’s home range
Design IV: Repeated, paired use and local availability measurements over time. i.e., Use and availability paired at every time step for every animal



Speaker Notes: When studying resource selection, An animal might select coniferous forest when establishing its home range (2nd order selection), but within that home range, it might spend most of its time in hardwood swamps (3rd order selection). Thomas and Taylor classified study designs based on whether we track individuals (Design II & III) or pool them at the population scale (Design I). Design I has no marked individuals, so selection is inferred at the population level. That is why it blurs into species distribution modelling

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Home Range and Space Use

Utilization Distribution (UD): the two-dimensional relative frequency distribution of an animal’s position over a given period (Van Winkle 1975).
Common Home Range Estimators:

Minimum Convex Polygon (MCP): Draws a polygon around the outermost locations. Highly sensitive to sample size and outliers.
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE): Fits bivariate normal kernels over points to create smooth probability density contours.
Local Nearest-Neighbor Convex Hull (LoCoH): A non-parametric method that constructs localized convex hulls around each point and its \(k-1\) neighbors. Excellent for identifying hard boundaries (e.g., rivers, fences).
Brownian Bridge Movement Model (BBMM): Integrates the path trajectory and elapsed time between consecutive telemetry points to model movement corridors.



Speaker Notes: A home range is not just a hard border; it is a continuous probability of use (the Utilization Distribution). MCP is the oldest estimator but is highly flawed because it overestimates area. KDE creates beautiful smooth contours but can smooth over boundaries. LoCoH is excellent for identifying barriers. Finally, Brownian Bridges incorporate the actual sequential trajectory of movement, modeling the path between consecutive locations.
An MCP gives you a boundary and no intensity. Kernel, LoCoH and Brownian bridge all give you a UD.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Simulate data









Six Florida panthers, 713 locations. And we know the truth: these tracks were generated with β_wetforest = 0.72 and β_dryforest = 2.18.


Left: a fourteen-class land cover map of a two hundred kilometre square with six panther trajectories drawn on it. Right: the proportion of wet forest within five kilometres, with the same trajectories.”
THE POINT OF SIMULATED DATA HERE is that you get a right answer to check against. In every real resource selection study in the literature, nobody knows these two numbers. Today you do.
The generating model is a step-selection process: at each step, 20 candidate steps are proposed from a gamma step-length distribution and a wrapped-normal turning-angle distribution, and one is chosen with probability proportional to exp(0.72 x wetforest + 2.18 x dryforest - 0.06 x distance from range centre).
TWO THINGS EMERGE rather than being imposed, and both matter later. Home ranges emerge from habitat selection plus weak centre attraction — nobody drew a boundary. And temporal autocorrelation emerges because each location depends on the last.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Design II: available is the whole study area
text:
Design II: available is the whole study area

set.seed(811)
e   <- ext(land)
av2 <- data.frame(x = runif(6000, xmin(e), xmax(e)),
                  y = runif(6000, ymin(e), ymax(e)))

d2 <- rbind(
  data.frame(used = 1, terra::extract(hab, tracks[, c("x", "y")])[, -1]),
  data.frame(used = 0, terra::extract(hab, av2)[, -1]))

m2 <- glm(used ~ wetforest + dryforest, data = na.omit(d2), family = binomial)
round(coef(m2)[-1], 3)


This is the classic use-availability RSF: used points against random points, fitted by logistic regression. It is by far the most common design in the wildlife literature.
WHY THE INTERCEPT IS DROPPED FROM THE PRINTOUT. It is not estimable in any meaningful sense — its value depends entirely on how many available points you chose to draw. Draw 60,000 instead of 6,000 and the intercept moves; the slopes do not. That is exactly the Candy Bowl result, now in a regression: you have an RSF, which is relative, not an RSPF, which is a probability.
Ask the room what would happen to the coefficients if we used 60,000 available points. Answer: essentially nothing, beyond tighter standard errors. Worth running live if someone doubts it — change one number and re-run.
