section: Design III: available is the animal’s home range
text:
Design III: available is the animal’s home range

set.seed(812)
av3 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cats, function(cid) {
  s  <- as.matrix(tracks[tracks$CatID == cid, c("x", "y")])
  pg <- mcp_poly(s, 95); bb <- apply(pg, 2, range)
  got <- matrix(nrow = 0, ncol = 2)
  while (nrow(got) < 1000) {                     # rejection sampling
    cd  <- cbind(runif(5000, bb[1, 1], bb[2, 1]),
                 runif(5000, bb[1, 2], bb[2, 2]))
    got <- rbind(got, cd[in_poly(cd, pg), , drop = FALSE])
  }
  data.frame(x = got[1:1000, 1], y = got[1:1000, 2])
}))

d3 <- rbind(
  data.frame(used = 1, terra::extract(hab, tracks[, c("x", "y")])[, -1]),
  data.frame(used = 0, terra::extract(hab, av3)[, -1]))

m3 <- glm(used ~ wetforest + dryforest, data = na.omit(d3), family = binomial)
round(coef(m3)[-1], 3)


Same used points. Same model. The only change is that available points now come from inside each cat’s own 95% MCP instead of the whole region.
THE MCP IS A CHOICE, AND IT IS DOING WORK. Swap it for a 95% kernel and the available set changes, so the coefficients change. Chapter 8’s estimator comparison is not an academic exercise — the estimator you pick to define the home range becomes an assumption inside your selection model.
in_poly() is the even-odd ray-casting rule in nine lines of base R: count how many polygon edges a ray from the point crosses; odd means inside. Worth showing once so point-in-polygon stops being a black box.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Design IV: available is the next step
text:
Design IV: available is the next step

make_ssf <- function(cid, n_ctrl = 10) {
  xy <- as.matrix(tracks[tracks$CatID == cid, c("x", "y")]); n <- nrow(xy)
  dx <- diff(xy[, 1]); dy <- diff(xy[, 2])
  sl <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)                       # observed step lengths
  ab <- atan2(dy, dx)                           # absolute bearings
  ta <- ((diff(ab) + pi) %% (2 * pi)) - pi      # observed turning angles
  idx <- 2:(n - 1); k <- length(idx)
  st  <- paste0(cid, "_", idx)
  slc <- sample(sl, k * n_ctrl, TRUE)           # draw FROM THE OBSERVED
  tac <- sample(ta, k * n_ctrl, TRUE)           #   distributions, not a disc
  aa  <- rep(ab[idx - 1], each = n_ctrl) + tac
  rbind(
    data.frame(stratum = st, used = 1, x = xy[idx + 1, 1], y = xy[idx + 1, 2]),
    data.frame(stratum = rep(st, each = n_ctrl), used = 0,
               x = rep(xy[idx, 1], each = n_ctrl) + slc * cos(aa),
               y = rep(xy[idx, 2], each = n_ctrl) + slc * sin(aa)))
}

set.seed(813)
d4 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cats, make_ssf))
d4 <- na.omit(cbind(d4, terra::extract(hab, d4[, c("x", "y")])[, -1]))

m4 <- clogit(used ~ wetforest + dryforest + strata(stratum), data = d4)
round(coef(m4), 3)


Each observed step is matched to 10 steps the cat could have taken instead, drawn from ITS OWN step-length and turning-angle distributions. Then conditional logistic regression compares within each matched set.
THIS IS GAUGE TRAP (g) DONE CORRECTLY. Available steps come from the observed step distribution, not uniformly from a buffer. An animal that mostly takes 5 km steps is not choosing uniformly inside a 15 km circle, and pretending otherwise biases every coefficient.
NO INTERCEPT AT ALL in a conditional logit — it cancels within each stratum. That is not a limitation here; the intercept was never interpretable anyway.
ONE HONEST CAVEAT worth stating if you have strong students: we draw available steps from the OBSERVED step lengths, but the observed lengths are themselves a selected sample of what was proposed. Forester et al. (2009) show this induces a small bias and recommend including step length as a covariate to absorb it. Our n_ctrl = 10 and a well-mixed landscape keep it minor, but it is real.

WHAT TO EXPECT, and what each outcome means.
Design IV should sit closest to the dashed truth lines, because its availability matches the generating process.
Designs II and III should both differ from truth and from each other. The direction is not guaranteed and depends on where the home-range centres happened to land relative to habitat, which in this simulation is essentially arbitrary. Which one recoverd the truth? THE ANSWER TO “why that one”: Design IV is the only design whose definition of available matches the process that generated the data. The simulation chose among candidate NEXT STEPS; Design IV compares against candidate next steps. Designs II and III compare against places the cat could not possibly have reached in one move.
THEN THE UNCOMFORTABLE FOLLOW-UP, which is the real lesson: with real panthers you do not know the generating process. You cannot check which design matches it. You pick one, and the picking determines your answer.

text:
Activity Debrief

The used points never changed. Only the available did.
Design IV won because its availability matched the process that generated the data — and in the field, you never get to check that.

Different orders. The two availability domains ask different questions.


In your own thesis you will have neither, and the availability domain will still be the single most consequential decision you make.
FIRST, coefficients of an exponential RSF fitted through a logistic regression package are NOT log-odds ratios. They are relative risk. The interpretation follows the model being fitted, not the software used to fit it.
SECOND, Manly’s used-versus-unused design with binary regression estimates probability of OCCUPANCY, not probability of selection. The RSF from a use-availability design and the RSPF from a used-unused design are not proportional to each other. They are different quantities that unfortunately inherited similar names.

## Point-in-polygon, base R only. Vectorised over points; loops over edges,
## which is cheap because a convex hull has ~15-25 vertices.
pip <- function(x, y, px, py) {
  n <- length(px)
  if (px[1] == px[n] && py[1] == py[n]) {          # drop the closing vertex
    px <- px[-n]; py <- py[-n]; n <- n - 1L
  }
  j <- c(n, seq_len(n - 1L))                       # previous vertex of each edge
  inside <- logical(length(x))
  for (k in seq_len(n)) {
    xi <- px[k];    yi <- py[k]
    xj <- px[j[k]]; yj <- py[j[k]]
    cross <- ((yi > y) != (yj > y)) &
             (x < (xj - xi) * (y - yi) / (yj - yi) + xi)
    inside <- xor(inside, cross)                   # odd number of crossings = in
  }
  inside
}
mcp_xy <- function(xy, pct = 95) {
  ctr  <- colMeans(xy)
  d    <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - ctr[1])^2 + (xy[, 2] - ctr[2])^2)
  keep <- xy[d <= quantile(d, pct / 100), , drop = FALSE]
  ch   <- chull(keep)
  rbind(keep[ch, ], keep[ch[1], ])
}

cat("\n=== Four availability domains ===\n")
n_av <- function(u) nrow(u) * 50L

avail_fun <- list(
  study_area = function(a, u) cbind(x = runif(n_av(u), X0, X0 + NX * RES),

  mcp_95 = function(a, u) {

    pts <- st_coordinates(st_sample(p, n_av(u), type = "random"))
    while (nrow(pts) < n_av(u))                      # st_sample can under-deliver
      pts <- rbind(pts, st_coordinates(st_sample(p, n_av(u), type = "random")))
    pts[seq_len(n_av(u)), 1:2]
  },
  kde_95 = function(a, u) {
    ah <- track[track$id == a, ]
    sample_from_ud(kde_grid(ah$x, ah$y, forest, h_ref(ah$x, ah$y)), 0.95, n_av(u))
  },
  bbmm_95 = function(a, u) {
    ah <- track[track$id == a, ]
    sample_from_ud(bbmm_grid(ah$x, ah$y, forest, bb_sigma2m(ah$x, ah$y)), 0.95, n_av(u))
  })

e2 <- t(sapply(names(avail_fun), function(nm) {
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(N_ANIMALS), function(a) {
    u  <- used_daily[used_daily$id == a, ]
    av <- avail_fun[[nm]](a, u)
    dd <- rbind(data.frame(id = a, x = u$x, y = u$y, case = 1L),
                data.frame(id = a, x = av[, 1], y = av[, 2], case = 0L))
    add_cov(dd, matrix(dens[a, ], nrow(dd), 2, byrow = TRUE))
  }))
  d <- d[complete.cases(d[, c("forest", "dist_water", "dist_den")]), ]
  d$wt <- ifelse(d$case == 1L, 1, 5000)
  m <- glm(case ~ forest + dist_water + dist_den, binomial, weights = wt, data = d)
  c(forest            = unname(coef(m)["forest"]),
    dist_water        = unname(coef(m)["dist_water"]),
    dist_den          = unname(coef(m)["dist_den"]),

}))
print(round(e2, 3))

    round(mean(rast_get(forest, used_daily$x, used_daily$y)), 3),
    "| true step-scale forest beta =", round(mean(b_forest_i), 3), "\n")

Questions:

If we plot the fourth column against the first. What is the relationship?
Johnson (1980) defined orders of selection. Label each of the four rows with an order, and say what question each one answers in plain English.
Which of these four is “correct”? Justify your answer in one sentence.


Expect study_area > mcp_95 ~ kde_95 > bbmm_95, tracking the mean availability of forest in the last column: the further the availability pool sits from the used points, the bigger the “selection”. Orders of selection: study_area mixes second (range placement) with third (within-range use); the others are closer to third. None of them equals the step-scale truth, and none is “correct” in the abstract, each answers a different question. This is the single most important idea.
Negative, and steep. Slope ≈ −4.2, r ≈ −0.77. As the availability pool becomes more like the used points, the apparent selection shrinks. Mean cover at used points is 0.722; all four denominators sit well below it (0.488 → 0.588), which is why all four report positive selection. The narrower the gap, the smaller the coefficient.
The clean version of the pattern is in the other two columns, not the first. dist_water is perfectly monotone: −0.578, −0.466, −0.374, −0.312, decaying toward zero as the denominator tightens. dist_den nearly so. These are the textbook demonstration that a coefficient is a contrast against a denominator you chose.
forest is deliberately the messy one, and that’s the more interesting finding. It is not monotone — mcp_95 has the largest coefficient (2.621) despite a more forested availability pool than study_area (0.508 vs 0.488). Two mechanisms, both worth putting to the class:
An MCP is convex by construction, so it swallows low-forest pockets inside the hull that the animal demonstrably never entered. Those are counted as available. A smaller region can therefore produce a stronger apparent preference than the whole study area. Mean availability alone doesn’t determine the coefficient — the shape of the availability distribution does. These are partial coefficients. forest, dist_water and dist_den are correlated, and the contrast in all three shifts together when you change domains. Look at dist_den: −3.131 under study-area availability versus −2.039 under the MCP. Part of what forest is doing under one denominator gets absorbed by dist_den under another.
The bonus result. Only bbmm_95 lands on the truth (2.066 against 2.088). Not luck in mechanism, though possibly in precision: a Brownian bridge availability domain is built from the movement process, so of the four it is the closest approximation to the step-scale denominator the data were actually generated under. That’s the thread into Exercise 5 — move the availability kernel toward the movement kernel and the RSF estimate moves toward the SSF estimate. With a single realisation and no confidence intervals on these four points, treat the exact agreement as suggestive; re-run with a different seed before claiming it in a lecture.
The thing students should not conclude is that BBMM is therefore “the right RSF.” It landed near the step-scale truth because this simulation generated data at the step scale. Had the question been about range placement, the study-area row would be the relevant answer and the BBMM row the misleading one.

              by, nrow(xy), h,

              ud_area_km2(kde_grid(xy[, 1], xy[, 2], forest, 150), 0.95)))
}


h_ref = sigma * n^(-1/6). What does the “n” in that formula assume about the fixes? Is that assumption true for a 1-hour GPS track?
Two studies report home ranges for the same species, one from VHF fixes every 3 days and one from GPS fixes every 15 min. Can you compare them?
Look up autocorrelated KDE (AKDE). What quantity does it substitute for n?


h_ref shrinks as n grows (n^(-1/6)), so hourly data give a spiky UD and a SMALLER 95% area than daily data, even though the animal’s range is identical. Holding h fixed largely removes the effect, which localises the problem in the bandwidth rule, not the kernel. The n in h_ref is an INDEPENDENT sample size; AKDE substitutes an effective sample size from a fitted continuous-time movement model (Fleming et al. 2015).

Q2 TARGET: Van Horne and the ecological trap. Selection is a behaviour, not a fitness measurement — without demography you have documented a preference, not established quality. Same gap Chapter 7 flagged between distributions and niches.
Q3 TARGET, straight from Lele et al.: to fit an RSPF rather than an RSF you need at least one CONTINUOUS covariate — with all-categorical covariates the probability of selection is not estimable at all — plus a substantial number of used points, generally 300 to 500 for stable estimates, and a non-exponential link such as logistic, probit or complementary log-log. The exponential model cannot deliver it, because its intercept is not estimable.
A student who writes “a continuous covariate and a few hundred points” has read the paper properly.
